Chapter 1 Instruction Set Architecture ​

Every program that runs on a robot ultimately reduces to fixed-width binary numbers moving between small hardware storage cells and memory addresses. The brain processor contract specifies the exact rules governing those binary instructions, storage containers, memory regions, and external timer or device interruptions. Building that hardware-software contract from first principles yields a self-contained, executable Python specification in oracle.py verified by test_oracle.py.

1. Software Golden Reference Models ​

When you write an ordinary program in Python or C, statements execute one after another in a single predictable sequence. A physical processor core (Central Processing Unit, or CPU) is instead built in a text-based circuit specification language (Hardware Description Language, or HDL) such as SystemVerilog. Under the hood, that description wires together elementary true/false switches (boolean logic gates), selector switches (multiplexers, the circuit equivalent of cond ? a : b), and clocked 1-bit storage cells (flip-flops). Between consecutive ticks of a periodic clock signal (one clock cycle), logic gates and multiplexers continuously compute new wire voltages in parallel, and on each tick all flip-flops sample those wires and update their stored bits at the exact same instant.

Testing a concurrent circuit design solely with hand-written test scripts mixes circuit timing with expected instruction behavior and leaves complex multi-instruction or external-signal corner cases unchecked. Processor teams separate those concerns before writing any circuit code by building an unambiguous sequential software specification called a golden reference model, or oracle, which is verified independently in software and then supplies automatic instruction-by-instruction expected states for arbitrary compiled programs. oracle.py implements that golden 32-bit reference specification for the brain CPU in the Python class Oracle, modeling the open-source fifth-generation processor standard built around a small, uniform set of simple 32-bit operations (Reduced Instruction Set Computer, Fifth Generation, or RISC-V). Before any hardware exists, unit tests in test_oracle.py verify the Python oracle's arithmetic bounds, memory-access rules, and timer alarms directly. Later, when our SystemVerilog CPU runs inside an open-source simulator that compiles circuit descriptions into fast C++ executables (Verilator), our verification harness feeds the exact same machine-code program to both engines in lockstep. After every completed (retired) instruction, hardware fault, or external interruption, Oracle.step() returns a structured step receipt recording updated internal CPU storage, next-instruction address, and memory state, so the harness can compare each receipt against the simulated hardware state and halt on the exact step where they diverge.

Instruction Set Architecture Boundaries ​

Every large software system relies on clean interface boundaries: a function signature tells callers what inputs a function accepts and what result it returns without exposing the temporary variables inside its body. In computer engineering, the boundary separating software (compilers, startup programs, control loops) from physical chip hardware (logic gates, wire routing, multi-cycle arithmetic units) is the Instruction Set Architecture, or ISA.

An ISA defines only what machine-code programs can observe between instructions:

  1. Architectural State: The persistent storage containers (fast on-chip storage cells called registers, the active instruction address, addressable memory, and modeled device state) whose values survive from one instruction to the next.
  2. Binary Instruction Encoding: The exact bit positions that pack an operation selector, register indices, and small constants into a fixed-width binary integer (a hardware word).
  3. Atomic Step Outcomes: Given any current architectural state St, step deterministically computes the next state St+1=step(St) through exactly one of two indivisible outcomes:
    • Normal Retirement: The current instruction completes cleanly, updating the active instruction address and committing the instruction's defined register or memory writes.
    • Precise Trap: An abrupt control-flow handover (trap) triggered by an illegal encoding, invalid memory access, or pending external/timer request aborts any partial writes of the current instruction and redirects execution to a dedicated handler address.

Because an ISA intentionally hides internal circuit timing—such as whether integer division takes one clock cycle or thirty-two clock cycles—oracle.py can model instruction execution sequentially in Python rather than cycle by cycle. To keep timer alarms and external interruptions equally reproducible without cycle-level simulation, the oracle advances its external hardware-device models at those same deterministic instruction boundaries. This separation lets us build and verify the complete software oracle independently before designing the physical circuit and running lockstep checks.

2. Fixed-Width Binary Arithmetic ​

In Python, evaluating 2**200 or -5 allocates a variable-length object in memory so integers grow until system memory runs out. Inside a physical CPU, there is no dynamic memory allocator for numbers. A 32-bit hardware register is 32 parallel metal wires driven by 32 flip-flops, where each wire carries either a low voltage representing zero or a high voltage representing one. Every loop counter, memory address, and sensor reading must fit inside those 232=4,294,967,296 distinct bit patterns, so arithmetic that steps past the ends of the representable range must obey a strict mathematical rule.

Bitwise Wire Gates and Bit Shifts ​

Every hardware register holds an ordered row of binary wires carrying 0 or 1 signals, read from left to right. On a 4-wire register holding 1011 (Bits 3..0), Bit 0 sits at the rightmost 1 and Bit 3 sits at the leftmost 1. Generalizing to any width of N wires labels individual wire bi∈{0,1} as Bit i (bN−1,…,b0) and any contiguous slice from bhi down to blo as Bits hi..lo.

Hardware combines and slides raw bit patterns across wires using six elementary operators: four bitwise gates (&, |, ^, ~) and two bit shifts (<<, >>). Each bitwise gate evaluates Bit i solely from Bit i of its inputs, while bit shifts slide every bit left or right across wire positions:

OperatorPython / Equation TokenSingle-Bit Rule (0 / 1)Primary Hardware Role
Bitwise ANDa & b1 only when both input bits equal 1Clears bits where a selector pattern (bitmask) holds 0, keeping bits where it holds 1
Bitwise ORa | b1 whenever either input bit equals 1Sets flag bits or combines non-overlapping packed fields
Bitwise Exclusive-OR (XOR)a ^ b / ⊕1 when the two input bits differToggles bits paired with 1 and leaves bits paired with 0 unchanged
Bitwise NOT~a / a¯Flips every bit (0 ↔ 1, a¯i=1−ai)Inverts all wires in parallel
Bitwise Left Shifta << k / ≪Slides every bit left by k positionsFills vacated bottom wires with 0 (or places 1 at Bit k via 1 << k)
Bitwise Right Shifta >> k / ≫Slides every bit right by k positionsDiscards bottom wires and zero-fills vacated top wires

Evaluating those rules concretely on four wires, Bitwise AND (1011 & 0011) zeroes the upper two bits where the mask holds 0 to keep 0011, while Bitwise Left Shift (1011 << 1) drops the leftmost 1 and fills Bit 0 with 0 to produce 0110.

Unsigned Binary Integers ​

Assigning base-two place weights 20,21,…,2N−1 from right to left maps an N-wire pattern with no dedicated sign wire onto non-negative integers. To write wide bit patterns compactly, programmers group every four wires (values 0–15) into one base-16 (hexadecimal) digit 0–9 (0–9) or A–F (10–15) prefixed with 0x, separating 4-digit groups with underscores. On a 4-bit register (N=4), place weights evaluate three sample patterns directly alongside their hexadecimal digits:

4-Bit PatternPlace-Weight SumUnsigned DecimalHexadecimal
00110⋅8+0⋅4+1⋅2+1⋅130x3
10111⋅8+0⋅4+1⋅2+1⋅1110xB
11111⋅8+1⋅4+1⋅2+1⋅1150xF

Pairing 1011 (0xB) with 0101 (0x5) therefore writes the 8-wire pattern 1011_0101 compactly as 0xB5.

Generalizing from 4 wires to any width N≥1 defines the unsigned integer interpretation UN(b):

UN(b)=∑i=0N−1bi⋅2i

When every wire carries zero, UN(b)=0; when every wire carries one, the finite geometric sum S=1+2+⋯+2N−1 satisfies 2S−S=2N−1, so the all-ones maximum equals ∑i=0N−12i=2N−1 (matching 1+2+4+8=15=24−1 on 4 bits). Because every bit sits in {0,1}, every N-bit unsigned integer lies inside [0,2N−1].

Distinct bit patterns never collide on the same unsigned integer: at the highest wire k where two patterns differ, all higher bits match and cancel, while the pattern carrying 1 at Bit k contributes 2k—strictly more than the maximum 2k−1 that all k lower wires combined can ever reach. Since all 2N distinct patterns land on distinct values inside the 2N-element interval [0,2N−1], UN is a one-to-one mapping (bijection) onto [0,2N−1]. For N=32, oracle.py names that upper bound UINT32_MAX = 0xFFFF_FFFF (232−1=4,294,967,295).

Binary Addition and Carry Propagation ​

Binary addition adds columns from Bit 0 upward using the exact same column-carry rule as base-ten arithmetic, rolling over at 2 rather than 10 whenever two input bits and any incoming carry sum to 2 or 3. Adding the 4-bit unsigned pair 1011 (11) and 0111 (7) passes a carry from Bit 0 up through Bit 3, spilling the Bit-3 carry-out (+16) off the left end and leaving 0010 (2) on the four output wires. The interactive 4-bit column adder below traces every carry wire across Bits 0 through 3 and lets you toggle inputs to see how carry-out drops off a fixed-width register.

4-Bit Binary Column Addition and Carry-Out Wrap-Around

Input B (Bits 3..0):
↔ Swipe horizontally to inspect every carry wire

On each column i, adding input bits ai,bi∈{0,1} and an incoming carry ci∈{0,1} (starting with c0=0) forms column total ti=ai+bi+ci∈{0,1,2,3}, emitting kept bit si∈{0,1} and outgoing carry ci+1∈{0,1} satisfying ai+bi+ci=si+2ci+1:

  • No Carry (ti∈{0,1}): Column sums 0 and 1 write si=ti with outgoing carry ci+1=0.
  • Generate Carry (ti∈{2,3}): Column sums 2 and 3 write si=ti−2 with outgoing carry ci+1=1.

Weighting each column identity by 2i and summing across all N≥1 wires shows that every internal carry ci⋅2i entering column i cancels the outgoing carry ci⋅2i leaving column i−1, leaving only the kept N-bit sum and the final carry past Bit N−1 (with no internal carries to cancel when N=1):

∑i=0N−1(ai+bi+ci)2i=∑i=0N−1si2i+∑i=0N−1ci+12i+1UN(a)+UN(b)+c0+∑i=1N−1ci2i=UN(s)+∑j=1N−1cj2j+cN2NUN(a)+UN(b)=cN⋅2N+UN(s)

Since 0≤UN(s)<2N and an N-bit register has only N output wires (Bits N−1..0), the final carry-out past Bit N−1 (cN∈{0,1} with place weight 2N) has no register wire to land on and drops off the left end.

Modular Rings and Congruence ​

Arithmetic on a fixed-width register works like counting around a circular clock face: instead of growing without bound, stepping past slot 15 on a 16-slot dial wraps back around to 0 (just as a 12-hour wall clock wraps back past 12). On 4-bit wires (0000 through 1111), 11+7=18 completes one full 16-slot lap plus 2 extra steps to land on slot 2 (18=1⋅16+2), while stepping backward 5 slots from slot 0 lands on slot 11 (−5=(−1)⋅16+11). Splitting any whole number into full m-slot laps (integer quotient q) plus a non-negative slot remainder r between 0 and m−1 defines integer division with a non-negative remainder (Euclidean division) around an m-slot cycle (modular ring). Two integers that differ by whole laps land on the exact same slot (residue class), written a≡b(modm)—for instance, 18≡2(mod16) and −5≡11(mod16).

16-Slot Unsigned Modular Clock (Modulo 16)

Every multiple of 16 completes one full clockwise lap around the 16-slot ring and lands back on the same slot. Try stepping past slot 15 or backward below 0, or click any slot directly.

Integer Input (x)
x = 18 (11 + 7 = 18)
Euclidean Division (m = 16)
18 = (1) × 16 + 2
4-Bit Hardware Remainder (Bits 3..0):0010 (2 unsigned)
Residue Class:18 ≡ 2 (mod 16)

Compactly, dividing any integer x∈Z by a positive integer modulus m>0 yields a unique integer quotient q and non-negative remainder r=xmodm inside the modular ring Zm:

x=q⋅m+r,0≤r<m,xmodm=r

Setting m=2N partitions any integer x into q dropped 2N-laps and the exact N-bit remainder r=xmod2N∈[0,2N−1] carried on wires 0 through N−1—matching our 4-bit adder where 18=1⋅16+2 leaves r=2 (0010) after dropping carry-out c4=1. Walking any m consecutive integers around an m-slot clock visits every slot exactly once, so two integers inside any single m-number window [a,a+m−1] share the same residue modulo m only when they are equal. Any two integers in [a,a+m−1] differ by strictly less than m, so their difference can be a multiple of m only when it equals zero.

Modular congruence passes cleanly through addition, subtraction, and multiplication for any positive modulus m, letting us swap congruent operands anywhere inside sums and products. On our 16-slot ring (m=16), swapping 19≡3(mod16) and 14≡−2(mod16) leaves both sum and product slots unchanged:

19+14=33≡3+(−2)=1(mod16)19⋅14=266≡3⋅(−2)=−6≡10(mod16)

In general, writing x=x′+k1m and y=y′+k2m (for integers k1,k2) keeps every extra term a multiple of m after adding, subtracting, or multiplying:

x±y=(x′±y′)+(k1±k2)m≡x′±y′(modm)x⋅y=x′y′+(k1y′+k2x′+k1k2m)m≡x′y′(modm)

Setting y=y′=c likewise shows integer scaling (c⋅x≡c⋅x′(modm)) preserves congruence. In practice, ≡(modm) acts as a drop-in substitution rule across +, −, and × once you respect four boundaries:

Congruence RuleRequirementValid vs. Broken Substitution
Safe Term-Wise SubstitutionReplace congruent terms under one shared modulus m across +, −, ×, and integer scalingSwapping 14→−2 modulo 16 preserves sums and products directly
Matching Terms and ModulusEvery swapped term must match modulo m without mixing distinct moduliSwapping 14→13 modulo 16 breaks 19+14=33≢16=3+13(mod16)
Integer DivisionDropping integer-division remainders breaks congruenceDividing 17≡1(mod16) by 5 drops remainders to quotients 3≢0
Factor CancellationCancelling a factor sharing a divisor >1 with m breaks congruence6⋅5≡6⋅13(mod16) yet 5≢13 because 6 and 16 share factor 2

Two's Complement Signed Integers ​

Robot control software also needs negative integers for joint velocity errors, signed sensor readings, and backward memory offsets. Dedicating the top wire as a separate sign flag—the intuitive sign-magnitude encoding—creates two zeros (0000 for +0 and 1000 for −0) and breaks ordinary binary addition: adding 0011 (+3) and 1101 (−5 in sign-magnitude) produces 0000 (0) instead of −2. Modern processors avoid both flaws with two's complement, reading negative integers counter-clockwise from zero on the modular clock ring so zero has a single representation and ordinary modular addition works unchanged across positive and negative numbers.

Starting at 0000 (0) on a 16-slot ring and stepping counter-clockwise by 1 lands on 1111 (15≡−1(mod16)), while stepping counter-clockwise by 5 lands on 1011 (11≡−5(mod16)). Algebraically, two's complement keeps positive place weights +20,…,+2N−2 on the lower N−1 wires and assigns the leftmost wire (Most Significant Bit, or MSB, at Bit N−1) a negative weight of −2N−1. On 4 bits, 1011 evaluates to −1⋅8+0⋅4+1⋅2+1⋅1=−5, and adding 0011 (+3) in ordinary binary gives 1011+0011=1110 (−8+4+2=−2), matching +3+(−5)=−2 directly. Whenever a true signed sum exits [−8,+7] across the discontinuity between +7 (0111) and −8 (1000)—stepping clockwise past +7 or counter-clockwise past −8—it wraps around the 16-slot clock to produce signed overflow, leaving addition modulo 16 unchanged.

The interactive 4-bit ring adder below displays both interpretations on the shared wheel—pairing raw bit toggles with unsigned (0..15) and signed (−8..+7) sums—before we generalize to N bits.

4-Bit Two's-Complement Shared Addition Clock

Think of a 4-bit register like a 16-slot clock face (0000 at 12 o'clock): outer numbers show unsigned values (0..15) and inner circles show two's-complement signed values (-8..+7), yet stepping clockwise by Input B's unsigned count computes both sums on the exact same binary adder.

Input A (Green Halo — Click Bits 3..0)

Input B (Amber Halo — Click Bits 3..0)

1011 + 0011 = 1110
Unsigned: 11 + 3 → 14
Signed: (-5) + (+3) → -2 (exact)
Inner ring: Signed · Outer ring: Unsigned

Generalizing that negative MSB weight to any bit width N≥1 defines the signed two's-complement interpretation SN(b):

SN(b)=−bN−1⋅2N−1+∑i=0N−2bi⋅2i

Splitting on the top sign wire confirms that every N-bit pattern maps uniquely onto one signed integer with a single zero (with no lower wires when N=1, giving S1(b0)=−b0∈{−1,0}). For N≥2, the lower N−1 wires span [0,2N−1−1] bijectively, so patterns with bN−1=0 cover [0,2N−1−1] (with zero unique at 00...0), while patterns with bN−1=1 shift downward by −2N−1 to cover [−2N−1,−1]. Together, SN maps all 2N patterns one-to-one onto the asymmetric interval [−2N−1,2N−1−1]. For N=32, oracle.py defines those endpoints using Python's left-shift syntax (1 << 31 places a single 1 bit at Bit 31 for 231) as INT32_MIN = -(1 << 31) (−2,147,483,648, bit pattern 0x8000_0000) and INT32_MAX = (1 << 31) - 1 (+2,147,483,647, bit pattern 0x7FFF_FFFF).

Because Python integers grow arbitrarily wide instead of wrapping at 32 wires, oracle.py projects every intermediate result back onto the 32-bit unsigned ring [0,232−1] using a single bitwise AND with 32 one-bits (MASK32 = 0xFFFF_FFFF). Python evaluates bitwise operators on any integer—positive, zero, or negative—as a two's-complement bit pattern wide enough to hold it (N≥33): every wire at Bit 32 or above carries an integer multiple of 232, while Bits 31..0 hold the non-negative remainder U32(b31..0)∈[0,232−1]. Masking with MASK32 places 1 on Bits 31..0 and 0 on Bit 32 and above, stripping every upper multiple of 232—including the negative sign wire—so x & MASK32 returns xmod232 directly. For example, −5=(−1)⋅232+(232−5) masks via -5 & 0xFFFF_FFFF to 0xFFFF_FFFB, and 0x1_0000_0002 & 0xFFFF_FFFF masks directly to 2. u32 implements that 32-bit modular projection in one line:

py
def u32(val: int) -> int:
    """Wrap an arbitrary Python integer into unsigned 32-bit range [0, 2^32 - 1] (mod 2^32)."""
    return val & MASK32

Unified Addition, Negation, and Subtraction ​

Comparing the unsigned sum UN(b) and signed sum SN(b) on the exact same N-bit wire pattern explains why a single modular arithmetic contract serves both unsigned and two's-complement integers across addition, negation, and subtraction. On our 4-bit pattern 1011, U4(1011)=11 and S4(1011)=−5, which differ by 11−(−5)=16=24. Because the lower N−1 wires carry identical positive weights under both readings, subtracting SN(b) from UN(b) leaves only the top wire's +2N−1 versus −2N−1 difference (2⋅bN−12N−1=bN−12N, valid for all N≥1):

SN(b)=UN(b)−bN−1⋅2N⟹UN(b)≡SN(b)(mod2N)

Both readings of every N-bit pattern therefore occupy the exact same slot on the 2N-hour modular clock. Because every slot corresponds to one unique bit pattern, any operation returning the correct unsigned residue modulo 2N simultaneously holds the exact wrapped signed answer:

  1. Sign-Agnostic Addition and Subtraction: Wrapping unsigned sums and differences produces identical output bits for signed operands because replacing any operand by a value congruent modulo 2N leaves ± unchanged modulo 2N. On 4-bit 1011 (11 unsigned, −5 signed) and 1110 (14 unsigned, −2 signed), both readings produce 1001 for addition and 1101 for subtraction:

    Operation & ReadingExact CalculationModulo-16 Residue4-Bit Output
    Unsigned add U4(+)11+14=2591001
    Signed add S4(+)(−5)+(−2)=−791001
    Unsigned sub U4(−)11−14=−3131101
    Signed sub S4(−)(−5)−(−2)=−3131101

    Because UN≡SN(mod2N), any modular operation outputting UN(w)≡UN(a)±UN(b)(mod2N) satisfies SN(w)≡SN(a)±SN(b)(mod2N) directly.

  2. Negation via Invert Plus One: Negating a two's-complement word flips every bit (~b) and adds 1—on 4 bits, flipping +5 (0101) to 1010 and adding 0001 lands directly on −5 (1011). Because flipping every bit turns each bi into 1−bi, the inverted pattern sums to the all-ones complement (2N−1)−UN(b), so adding 1 yields 2N−UN(b):

    UN(b¯)+1=(2N−1−UN(b))+1=2N−UN(b)≡−SN(b)(mod2N)

    Checking both boundary patterns confirms wrap-around cleanly: negating 00...0 produces 2N, which drops its carry-out to return 00...0, while negating extremal −2N−1 (1000 on 4 bits, or INT32_MIN 0x8000_0000 on 32 bits) produces +2N−1, which exceeds the maximum positive value 2N−1−1 by 1 and wraps modulo 2N right back to −2N−1.

  3. Subtraction via Invert Plus One: Modular subtraction a−b reuses that exact addition rule by inverting b (b¯) and adding an extra +1 into Bit 0. On 4-bit 1011 (−5) minus 1110 (−2), 1011+0001+0001=1101 (13 unsigned, −3 signed), because substituting Item 2's identity directly yields:

    UN(a)+UN(b¯)+1=UN(a)+(2N−UN(b))≡UN(a)−UN(b)≡SN(a)−SN(b)(mod2N)

The ISA payoff is decisive: even though unsigned integers ([0,2N−1]) and signed two's-complement integers ([−2N−1,2N−1−1]) assign different meanings whenever bN−1=1, one shared modular wrapping rule satisfies unsigned add, signed add, unsigned subtract, signed subtract, and two's-complement negation alike—eliminating signedness splits across addition and subtraction instructions.

Sign-Agnostic Left-Shift Scaling ​

Processors multiply both unsigned and two's-complement integers by powers of two using one zero-filling left shift (a≪k for shift distance 0≤k<N), sliding every bit k positions toward higher place weights and filling the vacated lower k positions with zero. Shifting 4-bit 1011 (11 unsigned, −5 signed) left by k=1 drops Bit 3 (1) and fills Bit 0 with 0 to give 0110 (+6):

InterpretationTrue Scaled ProductModulo-16 Residue4-Bit Output
Unsigned (U4)11⋅2=2260110
Signed (S4)(−5)⋅2=−1060110

Shifting left by k multiplies every surviving lower bit ai (0≤i≤N−1−k) by 2k while discarding the top k bits whose shifted place weights 2i+k (i≥N−k) are all integer multiples of 2N:

UN(a≪k)=2kUN(a)−2N∑i=N−kN−1ai2i+k−N≡2kUN(a)(mod2N)

Because UN≡SN(mod2N) passes through scaling by 2k, the exact same bit pattern satisfies SN(a≪k)≡2kSN(a)(mod2N) (with k=0 leaving a unchanged). For signed values, left-shifting by k (1≤k<N) stays exact whenever all k discarded top bits match the incoming sign bit at Bit N−1−k (making Bits N−1..N−1−k all 0 or all 1). When those leading bits are all 0, the remaining N−1−k lower bits keep SN(a)∈[0,2N−1−k−1]. When they are all 1, the negative MSB combines with the k upper 1 weights across Bits N−2..N−1−k, whose finite sum equals 2N−1−2N−1−k:

−2N−1+∑i=N−1−kN−22i=−2N−1+(2N−1−2N−1−k)=−2N−1−k

That collapse keeps SN(a)∈[−2N−1−k,−1] (matching −2N−1+2N−2=−2N−2 when k=1), so 2kSN(a) remains exact inside [−2N−1,2N−1−1] across both cases. On 4 bits, 1101 (S4=−3, with Bit 3 and Bit 2 both 1) therefore shifts left by 1 cleanly to 1010 (S4=−6). As soon as a discarded bit differs from that incoming sign bit—such as 4-bit 1001 (S4=−7, where Bit 3 is 1 while Bit 2 is 0)—shifting left by 1 produces 0010 and wraps −14 around the 16-slot ring to +2. One zero-filling left-shift instruction therefore scales both unsigned and signed operands identically, whereas operations that break modular congruence split into separate unsigned and signed instructions in Section 4.

3. Core Registers and Instruction Encoding ​

With fixed-width binary arithmetic established, we can define the core processor storage initialized in Oracle.reset() and organize how a 32-bit machine word encodes operations, registers, and embedded constants. Separating core registers and instruction bit layouts from external memory and hardware timers keeps instruction decoding self-contained before adding attached devices.

Program Counter and Hardwired Zero Register ​

A CPU requires one dedicated register to track the active address in a running program and a small bank of fast working variables. Keeping that sequential instruction pointer separate from working data registers isolates control-flow state from arithmetic operands. Core integer execution therefore revolves around two fast storage structures inside the CPU:

  1. Program Counter (PC): self.pc, a single 32-bit register holding the memory byte address of the next instruction to fetch.
  2. General-Purpose Register File: self.regs, an array of 32 fast 32-bit integer registers named x0 through x31 (128 bytes of storage in total).

Choosing 32 registers rather than 8 or 256 balances fast access against instruction bit budget. Naming one of 32 registers takes log2⁡(32)=5 bits, so specifying one destination register (rd) and two source registers consumes 3×5=15 bits of a 32-bit instruction word and leaves 17 bits for operation selectors and embedded constants.

By ISA contract, reading register x0 always returns zero, and any write targeting x0 (rd == 0) is silently discarded. The golden reference model captures this discard rule directly in Oracle._set_reg:

py
    def _set_reg(self, rd: int, val: int) -> int:
        """Write `u32(val)` to `rd` (`x0` stays hardwired to `0`) and return the committed word."""
        if rd == 0:
            return 0
        u_val = u32(val)
        self.regs[rd] = u_val
        return u_val

Dedicating one register index permanently to zero keeps the instruction set compact without losing expressiveness. Assemblers and compilers reuse standard instructions with x0 as a constant zero source or a safe discard destination to clear, copy, or negate values, eliminating separate dedicated instructions.

Six Functional Instruction Families ​

The brain CPU executes instructions belonging to six functional groups, each solving a core programming need in oracle.py using the open RISC-V hardware specification. The 32-bit Base Integer (RV32I) instruction set handles arithmetic, control flow, and memory access, while Integer Multiply and Divide (RV32M) adds single-instruction multiplication and division. Combining the base integer set with the multiply-divide extension defines the RV32IM target implemented by our simulator and processor. System management adds special processor-control instructions to read hardware settings and handle external or timer alert (interrupt) state, while a custom neural extension adds domain acceleration for real-time motor inference.

GroupFunctional CategoryEveryday Programming Role
1Integer Arithmetic, Shifts, and ConstantsInteger math, bit masks, shifts, comparisons, and 32-bit constants
2Hardware Multiply and DivideUp to 64-bit integer products, plus 32-bit quotients and remainders
3Memory Loads and StoresReading and writing 8-bit, 16-bit, and 32-bit values in memory and devices
4Conditional Branches and JumpsLoops, if/else branches, direct calls, and function-pointer jumps
5System and Control RegistersSystem calls, debugger breakpoints, enabling or disabling timer and device interrupts, and cycle counters
6Custom Neural Multiply-AccumulateTwo-lane clamped dot products for real-time robot motor control

Bitfield Layouts and Offset Reach ​

The CPU decoder slices each fetched 32-bit unsigned word (insn) into register indices, operation selectors, and embedded constants before execution (writing insn[hi..lo] for Bits hi..lo of insn). In human-readable textual notation (assembly syntax), instructions list destination register rd first followed by source registers rs1 and rs2, as in Add (add rd, rs1, rs2), whereas instructions carrying a literal constant (immediate, or imm) replace rs2 with that constant, as in Add Immediate (addi rd, rs1, imm).

All standard 32-bit RISC-V primary operation codes (opcode, Bits 6..0) end with Bits 1..0 equal to binary 0b11 (decimal 3), reserving the other three 2-bit endings for optional 16-bit compressed instructions. Alongside opcode, instructions reuse two secondary sub-operation selectors—a 3-bit function code (funct3, Bits 14..12) and a 7-bit function code (funct7, Bits 31..25)—to distinguish individual operations sharing the same primary opcode. Every 32-bit instruction conforms to one of six standard bitfield layouts (Register / R-type, Immediate / I-type, Store / S-type, Branch / B-type, Upper Immediate / U-type, and Jump / J-type) that pack register indices, selectors, and signed offsets (omitting an always-zero Bit 0 on branch and jump targets as detailed right after the layout table) or upper constants across Bits 31..0. The wire matrix below aligns all six 32-bit RISC-V layouts across Columns 31..0 so you can inspect pinned register columns, the Bit 31 sign bit (S), and immediate or offset slices side by side before reading the exact bit mappings.

Notice two quantitative properties embedded directly in the bitfield layout table above:

  1. Offset Reach Scaling: An unscaled 12-bit signed immediate spans [−211,211−1], or [−2,048,+2,047] bytes (about ±2 KB), while an unscaled 20-bit signed immediate spans [−219,219−1] bytes. Because optional 16-bit compressed RISC-V instructions sit on even 2-byte addresses, the difference between any two instruction addresses is even (guaranteeing Bit 0 equals zero), letting the ISA drop Bit 0 and double byte reach onto even offsets without spending an instruction bit. Consequently, B-type encodes 12 stored bits to cover 2×[−211,211−1] ([−4,096,+4,094] even bytes, about ±4 KB), while J-type encodes 20 stored bits to cover 2×[−219,219−1] ([−1,048,576,+1,048,574] even bytes, about ±1 MB). Because the brain CPU implements only fixed 32-bit instructions without 16-bit compressed encodings, the RISC-V specification tightens runtime fetch alignment to 32 bits, or 4-byte multiples (Instruction Address Alignment, or IALIGN = 32).
  2. Pinned Columns and Shared Offset Slices: The encoding places register indices (rs1 at 19..15, rs2 at 24..20, rd at 11..7) and the immediate sign bit (Bit 31) in stationary columns across every format. Pinning those columns lets any decoder slice all register indices and sign bits uniformly before branching on opcode. Even further, B-type shares 11 of its 12 stored immediate bits with S-type (insn[31] as sign, insn[30..25] as Bits 10..5, and insn[11..8] as Bits 4..1), repurposing only insn[7] from S-type Bit 0 to B-type Bit 11. Similarly, J-type shares Bits 19..12 (insn[19..12]) with U-type and Bits 10..1 (insn[30..21]) with I-type.

Because register columns (rd at 11..7, rs1 at 19..15, rs2 at 24..20) and selector columns (opcode at 6..0, funct3 at 14..12, funct7 at 31..25) stay pinned across formats, Oracle.step() slices all six fields upfront before dispatching on opcode (formats omitting a field simply ignore its pre-sliced bits). To pull an upper bitfield down to Bit 0, an unsigned right shift (insn >> lo) moves every bit right by lo positions, discarding the lowest lo bits and zero-filling the vacated upper slots on non-negative words like insn (signed right shifts arrive with arithmetic instructions in Section 4). Inside Oracle.step(), combining that right shift with a w-bit mask 2w−1 (holding 1 in Bits w−1..0 and 0 above) clears every higher bit in parallel. Grouping those masks by field width—7-bit OPCODE_MASK = 0x7F and FUNCT7_MASK = 0x7F, 5-bit REG_MASK = 0x1F, and 3-bit FUNCT3_MASK = 0x7—extracts all six fields in six lines:

py
        opcode = insn & OPCODE_MASK
        rd = (insn >> 7) & REG_MASK
        funct3 = (insn >> 12) & FUNCT3_MASK
        rs1 = (insn >> 15) & REG_MASK
        rs2 = (insn >> 20) & REG_MASK
        funct7 = (insn >> 25) & FUNCT7_MASK

In oracle.py, enc_r, enc_i, enc_s, enc_b, enc_u, and enc_j assemble bit-exact test instructions across all six formats. These encoders position each field with left shifts (<<) and merge non-overlapping slices with bitwise OR (|). During execution, _dec_imm_s, _dec_imm_b, and _dec_imm_j reassemble those permuted slices into signed Python integers (whose bit-widening rule we explain in Widening Narrow Signed and Unsigned Integers).

Widening Narrow Signed and Unsigned Integers ​

Instruction decoders unpack narrow 12-bit, 13-bit, and 21-bit immediate payloads that expand to full 32-bit operands. When widening a narrow integer from k≥1 bits to a strictly wider word of M>k bits, sign extension preserves the signed value across all bit widths by copying the sign bit into every added upper position, whereas zero extension preserves unsigned values while corrupting negative numbers. For example, widening 12-bit −5 (0xFFB, with U12=4,091 and sign bit (Bit 11) equal to 1) to 32 bits separates the two rules cleanly:

Widening Rule32-Bit WordUnsigned (U32)Signed (S32)
Zero-extend 0xFFB0x0000_0FFB4,091+4,091
Sign-extend 0xFFB0xFFFF_FFFB232−5−5

The interactive wire schematic below shows 4-bit to 8-bit widening—contrasting constant-0 tie-offs against sign-bit copying across added upper lanes—before we verify both rules for arbitrary target width M>k.

Padding Bits M−1..k with zero adds zero place weight above Bit k−1, keeping the unsigned value unchanged (UM=Uk) while clearing the new top sign bit (Bit M−1) to 0. That zero sign bit forces the wider signed reading to match Uk(b)=Sk(b)+bk−12k, shifting negative numbers upward by 2k and preventing one shared widening rule from preserving both unsigned and signed values.

Conversely, replicating Bit k−1 into every added upper position preserves the exact signed value (SM=Sk) across arbitrary widths M>k. Widening a k-bit pattern b by a single bit to k+1 bits (b′, setting bk′=bk−1) replaces the old negative weight −bk−12k−1 with −bk−12k+bk−12k−1, which collapses right back to −bk−12k−1:

Sk+1(b′)=−bk−12k+bk−12k−1+∑i=0k−2bi2i=−bk−12k−1+∑i=0k−2bi2i=Sk(b)

Repeating that single-bit copy up to any target width M>k keeps SM(extended b)=Sk(b) for every k≥1 (with no lower sum when k=1), while shifting the unsigned reading of negative inputs upward by bk−1(2M−2k) since UM=SM+bk−12M=Uk−bk−12k+bk−12M.

Because the Python oracle stores raw bit patterns as unsigned integers (0..0xFFFF_FFFF in self.regs) and extracts field slices in _dec_imm_s, _dec_imm_b, and _dec_imm_j as non-negative values, Python operators such as <, +, -, and * would read 0xFFB as +4,091 and 0xFFFF_FFFB as +4,294,967,291 instead of −5. Correct signed comparisons, backward offsets, and arithmetic inside Python therefore require converting raw k-bit bit patterns into Python's native signed int representation (Sk(b)). Whereas a fixed 32-bit word widens a k-bit integer by replicating Bit k−1 across Bits 31..k, Python's arbitrary-precision integers have no top bit boundary to fill, so copying sign bits leaves negative two's-complement patterns strictly positive. Instead, the oracle masks the input down to its low k bits with 2k−1, flips Bit k−1 (s=2k−1) with bitwise XOR (^ in Python and ⊕ in equations), and subtracts s to shift negative inputs directly into Python's native signed range. Evaluating both 12-bit branches (s=211=0x800=2,048) shows how XOR shifts non-negative inputs upward by +s (cancelled by subtracting s) and negative inputs downward by −s (turning +211 into −211):

Sign Bit (Bit 11)12-Bit Input (v)Flip Sign Bit (v⊕0x800)Subtract 0x800 (2,048)
00x005 (+5)0x805 (2,053)+5
10xFFB (4,091)0x7FB (2,043)−5

Writing the masked k-bit value as v=bk−1s+L (where L=∑i=0k−2bi2i, or 0 when k=1) confirms the formula for every width k≥1, since XORing with s flips only bk−1 to 1−bk−1:

(v⊕s)−s=((1−bk−1)s+L)−s=−bk−1s+L=Sk(b)

In oracle.py, sign_extend binds 2k−1 to mask and 2k−1 to sign_bit to evaluate (val ^ sign_bit) - sign_bit on masked input val, and s32 specializes that helper to 32-bit words:

py
def sign_extend(val: int, bits: int) -> int:
    """Sign-extend `bits`-wide `val` via `(val ^ (1 << (bits - 1))) - (1 << (bits - 1))`."""
    # Flipping the top sign bit (Most Significant Bit / MSB) swaps [0..2^(bits-1)-1] and
    # [2^(bits-1)..2^bits-1]; subtracting 2^(bits-1) maps [0..2^bits-1] onto signed range.
    sign_bit = 1 << (bits - 1)
    mask = (1 << bits) - 1
    val &= mask
    return (val ^ sign_bit) - sign_bit


def s32(val: int) -> int:
    """Interpret lower 32 bits as signed two's complement: S_32(b) = U_32(b) - b_31 * 2^32."""
    return sign_extend(val, 32)

4. Integer Arithmetic, Multiplication, and Division ​

Once the decoder slices an instruction word, integer operations compute a 32-bit result strictly from the captured operand values and instruction selectors. Before executing any operation, Oracle.step() reads and holds both prior source register values (rs1_u, rs2_u = self.regs[rs1], self.regs[rs2]) and derives signed views via s32 (rs1_s, rs2_s). Because source values are captured before writing the result to rd, an in-place addition such as add x3, x3, x3 (adding x3 to itself) reads the prior x3 on both inputs and writes double that value back to x3.

Base Integer Operations and Zero Idioms ​

Every integer instruction set pairs two-register arithmetic (for dynamic variables) with register-immediate operations so programs can apply loop increments, bit masks, and bounds checks without spending an extra register to hold a small constant. Combining Section 3's primary opcode (Bits 6..0) with secondary function-selector fields funct3 (Bits 14..12) and funct7 (Bits 31..25), valid base integer instructions execute cleanly in one step, while any unassigned pattern aborts before modifying rd and routes to Section 1's atomic trap handler. In oracle.py, _exec_op_imm executes register-immediate integer instructions (opcode 0x13), while _exec_op_reg executes register-register instructions (opcode 0x33).

Across the base operations table below, write op2_u for the 32-bit unsigned second operand (rs2_u in register-register instructions or u32(imm) after sign-extending 12-bit imm in register-immediate instructions) and op2_s for its signed view (s32(op2_u)). Because architectural registers self.regs[rd] store raw 32-bit unsigned patterns (0..0xFFFF_FFFF), the oracle normalizes arithmetic and shift outputs through u32(...) while preserving signed views via Section 2's modular congruence. For shifts, RISC-V defines a 5-bit unsigned shift amount (shamt, 0 to 31) via rs2_u & 0x1F in register shifts (wrapping 35 & 31 to 3 via 0x1F = 31) or insn[24..20] in immediate shifts (leaving Bits 31..25 free for funct7). In Python's reference formulas inside the table below, rs1_u >> shamt models zero-filling right shifts, whereas u32(rs1_s >> shamt) wraps Python's signed downward-rounded right shift to match Bit 31 replication (a correspondence explained in Right Shifts and Integer Floor Division).

CategoryRegister / Immediate MnemonicSelector (funct3 / funct7)32-Bit Output Stored in rdKey Architectural Rule
Add / Subtractadd, addi / sub0 / 0x00 (R-type; sub: 0x20)u32(rs1_u + op2_u) / u32(rs1_u - rs2_u)Shared modular arithmetic; sub inverts rs2_u and adds 1; negative constants use addi
Shift Left Logicalsll, slli1 / 0x00u32(rs1_u << shamt)Zero-fills low bits; shamt is rs2_u & 0x1F or insn[24..20]; invalid funct7 traps
Shift Right Logicalsrl, srli5 / 0x00rs1_u >> shamtZero-fills upper bits (unsigned divide by 2shamt); invalid funct7 traps
Shift Right Arithmeticsra, srai5 / 0x20u32(rs1_s >> shamt)Replicates Bit 31 into upper bits (signed downward-rounded divide by 2shamt); invalid funct7 traps
Set Less Than (Signed)slt, slti2 / 0x00 (R-type)1 if rs1_s < op2_s else 0Compares signed views rs1_s and op2_s
Set Less Than (Unsigned)sltu, sltiu3 / 0x00 (R-type)1 if rs1_u < op2_u else 0sltiu sign-extends 12-bit imm first, so −1 becomes 0xFFFF_FFFF (UINT32_MAX, 232−1)

Assembly ShorthandUnderlying Machine EncodingArchitectural Effect

Right Shifts and Integer Floor Division ​

Shifting every bit right by 1≤k≤N−1 positions discards the lower k bits and leaves the top k positions (Bits N−1…N−k) empty, forcing the ISA to split into srl/srli and sra/srai (unlike addition, subtraction, or sll/slli). A logical right shift (b≫logk) fills those upper positions with zeros to divide unsigned values by 2k, whereas an arithmetic right shift (b≫arithk) replicates original sign bit bN−1 to preserve the sign of two's-complement values. One shared right-shift rule cannot serve both instructions because zero-filling a negative two's-complement word flips its sign bit to positive, whereas sign-replicating a large unsigned word injects phantom high bits.

Both right shifts match exact division rounded downward toward −∞ (floor division ⌊x/d⌋, where the floor ⌊y⌋ is the unique integer satisfying ⌊y⌋≤y<⌊y⌋+1). Shifting 4-bit 1011 (11 unsigned, −5 signed) right by k=1 drops Bit 0 (1) and separates the two fill rules cleanly:

Right-Shift Rule4-Bit OutputFloor-Division Reading
Logical (1011≫log1)0101U4=5=⌊11/2⌋
Arithmetic (1011≫arith1)1101S4=−3=⌊−5/2⌋

Why does dropping the low k bits always round downward toward −∞, even for negative numbers? For k=0, no bits drop and both shifts leave x=⌊x/1⌋ untouched; for 1≤k≤N−1, split b at Bit k into the kept (N−k)-bit upper slice H (Hj=bj+k, top bit bN−1) and the non-negative dropped remainder R=∑m=0k−1bm2m∈[0,2k−1]. Factoring 2k out of Bits N−1…k writes both interpretations as a shifted upper slice plus R:

UN(b)=UN−k(H)⋅2k+RSN(b)=SN−k(H)⋅2k+R

Because b≫logk zero-extends H while b≫arithk sign-extends H to N bits—holding through k=N−1 where S1(H)=−bN−1—Section 3's widening rules preserve both values at full width:

UN(b)=UN(b≫logk)⋅2k+RSN(b)=SN(b≫arithk)⋅2k+R

Writing (x,q) for either pair gives x=q⋅2k+R, and dividing 0≤R<2k by 2k bounds the fractional remainder inside 0≤R/2k<1. Adding q traps x/2k=q+R/2k inside [q,q+1), which by definition forces the integer quotient q=⌊x/2k⌋:

q≤q+R2k=x2k<q+1⟹q=⌊x2k⌋

That also closes our Python oracle formula from the base-operations table in Base Integer Operations and Zero Idioms: Python's rs1_s >> shamt computes ⌊S32(b)/2shamt⌋=S32(b≫arithshamt), so wrapping through u32(rs1_s >> shamt) recovers the exact 32-bit pattern via U32≡S32(mod232). On 32-bit 0xFFFF_FFFB (−5 signed, 232−5 unsigned), shifting right by k=1 drops Bit 0 (R=1) and highlights the sign split:

InstructionShifted 32-Bit OutputDecimal Value
srai (0xFFFF_FFFB≫arith1)0xFFFF_FFFD−3 (signed, not −2)
srli (0xFFFF_FFFB≫log1)0x7FFF_FFFD+2,147,483,645 (unsigned)

Whenever bN−1=1 and 1≤k≤N−1, srl fills every vacated upper bit (Bits N−1…N−k) with 0 while sra fills those exact same positions with 1, guaranteeing distinct bit patterns (whose unsigned values differ by 2N−2N−k per Section 3's sign-extension rule) and requiring two separate shift instructions.

Equality and Ordered Comparisons ​

Whether two register operands match under equality (==) never depends on signedness, whereas whether one operand is strictly less than another (<, requiring separate slt/slti versus sltu/sltiu instructions) flips whenever their top sign bits differ. For example, comparing a equal to 1011 (a3=1) against b equal to 0011 (b3=0) leaves U4(1011)=11>3=U4(0011) under unsigned comparison, yet pulls S4(1011)=−5<+3=S4(0011) under signed comparison. Because both UN onto [0,2N−1] and SN onto [−2N−1,2N−1−1] are one-to-one bijections on the 2N bit patterns, UN(a)=UN(b) and SN(a)=SN(b) both hold if and only if bit patterns a and b match bit-for-bit, requiring only one unsigned equality rule.

For ordered comparisons (< and ≥), substituting SN(x)=UN(x)−xN−1⋅2N relates the signed and unsigned differences in one line:

SN(a)−SN(b)=(UN(a)−UN(b))−(aN−1−bN−1)2N

When two patterns share the same top bit (aN−1=bN−1), the 2N term vanishes and signed and unsigned ordering match identically. When their top bits differ (aN−1=1 and bN−1=0), unsigned weights place UN(a)≥2N−1>UN(b), whereas the negative Most Significant Bit pulls SN(a)<0≤SN(b) so signed comparison reverses direction (and symmetrically when aN−1=0 and bN−1=1).

Watch one subtle ordering rule on immediate unsigned comparison sltiu rd, rs1, -1 (imm equal to 12-bit 0xFFF): the ISA always sign-extends the 12-bit immediate to 32-bit 0xFFFF_FFFF (UINT32_MAX) before performing the unsigned comparison, so rs1 holding 0xFFFF_FFFC (232−4) satisfies 0xFFFF_FFFC < 0xFFFF_FFFF and writes 1 into rd rather than comparing against 0x0000_0FFF. Sharing that single sign-extending immediate rule across every I-type instruction keeps immediate unpacking uniform across all base operations rather than special-casing sltiu.

Base Integer Signedness Equivalence ​

With all six fundamental base integer operation classes examined, algebraic invariance determines cleanly when one instruction rule serves both unsigned and signed interpretations versus when operations must split. The table below summarizes all six operation classes across Sections 2–4 (multiplication and division follow in Full 64-Bit Integer Multiplication and Truncating Integer Division Semantics):

OperationSame Bits for Unsigned & Signed?Algebraic and Contract Reason
Equality (==, !=)YesBoth UN and SN are one-to-one bijections, so values match if and only if bit patterns match
Add / Subtract (+, −)YesUN(b)≡SN(b)(mod2N) passes through ±
Left Shift (≪)YesDiscards multiples of 2N; shifts factor 2k on residue class
Ordered Compare (<, ≥)NoSubtracting bN−12N pulls bN−1=1 patterns below zero (11>3 versus −5<+3)
Widening (k→32 bits)NoZero-fill preserves Uk(b) while sign-bit replication preserves Sk(b)
Right Shift (≫)NoFor 1≤k≤N−1 and bN−1=1, srl writes 0 while sra writes 1 into Bits N−1…N−k

Full 32-Bit Constant Construction ​

Because every 32-bit instruction spends at least 12 bits on opcode and non-immediate control or register fields, no single instruction can embed an arbitrary 32-bit constant inside itself. Instead, RISC-V provides two U-type instructions that place a 20-bit immediate (imm20) into Bits 31..12 of rd while clearing Bits 11..0 to zero: Load Upper Immediate (lui) writes imm20 << 12, and Add Upper Immediate to PC (auipc) writes u32(cur_pc + (imm20 << 12)), where cur_pc denotes the current instruction's self.pc. When source code or assembly requests an arbitrary 32-bit constant via a pseudoinstruction such as li x5, value, the compiler or assembler computes a 20-bit upper payload hi_lui and a 12-bit offset lo12 offline ahead of execution and emits two real machine instructions—lui x5, hi_lui followed by addi x5, x5, lo12—while the processor executes those two standard instructions verbatim at runtime without special bias instructions.

Why can the compiler or assembler not simply copy Bits 31..12 straight into lui and Bits 11..0 straight into addi? Because addi sign-extends its 12-bit immediate before adding: Bits 11..0 act as non-negative offsets 0 through +2,047 when Bit 11 equals 0 (0x000–0x7FF), whereas Bits 11..0 act as negative offsets -2,048 through -1 (subtracting 0x1000, or 4,096, from their unsigned value) whenever Bit 11 equals 1 (0x800–0xFFF). A naive split on 0x1234_5ABC (Bit 11 equals 1) would emit lui x5, 0x12345 and addi x5, x5, -1348 (0xABC - 0x1000 = -0x544), which executes 0x1234_5000 - 0x544 = 0x1234_4ABC and undershoots by 0x1000.

To cancel that -0x1000 drop whenever Bit 11 equals 1 with one uniform offline recipe, the compiler or assembler runs two ordered steps:

  1. Step 1 (Extract Unbiased lo12): Slice Bits 11..0 directly from the original target constant before adding any bias.
  2. Step 2 (Bias and Slice hi_lui): Add 0x800 (2,048, half of 0x1000) to the target constant modulo 232, discard the altered low 12 bits of that sum, and take Bits 31..12 as hi_lui.

Two concrete constants trace both branches—notice how the bit-boundary diagram below tracks both fields across the Bit 11 to Bit 12 seam:

  • No Carry (0x1234_5123, Bit 11 = 0): Step 1 extracts lo12 = 0x123 (+291); Step 2 adds 0x800 without carrying past Bit 11, yielding hi_lui = 0x12345 so lui + addi compute 0x1234_5000 + 0x123 = 0x1234_5123.
  • Carry +1 (0x1234_5ABC, Bit 11 = 1): Step 1 extracts lo12 = 0xABC (-1,348, or -0x544); Step 2 adds 0x800, carries +1 into Bit 12, and promotes hi_lui to 0x12346 so runtime pre-bumps x5 to 0x1234_6000 and subtracts 0x544 to land on 0x1234_5ABC.
32-Bit Constant Split Carry Bias (+0x800 across Bit 11 to Bit 12)
↔ Swipe horizontally to inspect both Bit 11 cases

Checking the algebra confirms this two-step recipe reconstructs every 32-bit target X∈[0,232−1] exactly modulo 232. Split X at Bit 12 as X=hi20⋅212+U12(lo12), with Bit 11 denoted b11∈{0,1}. Adding 0x800 (211) carries +1 into Bit 12 if and only if U12(lo12)≥211 (b11=1), so hi_lui = u32(X + 0x800) >> 12 equals (hi20+b11)mod220. Because shifting any multiple of 220 left by 12 bits produces a multiple of 232 that drops off past Bit 31, combining lui with sign-extended addi (S12(lo12)=U12(lo12)−b11⋅212) cancels the ±b11⋅212 carry directly:

hi_lui⋅212+S12(lo12)≡(hi20+b11)⋅212+(U12(lo12)−b11⋅212)=hi20⋅212+U12(lo12)=X(mod232)

Two tight boundary checks confirm that 0x800 is exact down to a single unit. Near UINT32_MAX (X = 0xFFFF_F800), adding 0x800 wraps u32(0xFFFF_F800 + 0x800) cleanly to 0, emitting lui x5, 0x00000 and addi x5, x5, -2048 so runtime evaluates u32(0 - 2048) = 0xFFFF_F800. Conversely, shrinking the bias by just 1 to 0x7FF fails on 0x0000_1800 because 0x1800 + 0x7FF = 0x1FFF misses the Bit 12 carry and undershoots to 0x0800. Applying that exact same offline 0x800 split to the 32-bit wrapped PC-relative offset u32(target - cur_pc) and emitting auipc followed by addi lets compiled programs reach any address relative to self.pc across the entire 32-bit address space.

Full 64-Bit Integer Multiplication ​

Multiplying two 32-bit integers spans up to 64 bits across unsigned, signed, and mixed operands, yet each instruction in the Integer Multiply and Divide extension (RV32M, opcode 0x33, funct7 0x01) writes one 32-bit register rd. RISC-V therefore splits every 64-bit product into one shared lower-word instruction (Multiply, or mul, whose Bits 31..0 match across every signedness mode) and three upper-word instructions (Multiply High mulh, Multiply High Signed-Unsigned mulhsu, and Multiply High Unsigned mulhu). Unsigned-by-signed multiplication needs no fourth upper instruction because swapping rs1 and rs2 reduces U32(a)S32(b)=S32(b)U32(a) directly to mulhsu:

Instructionfunct3Operands (rs1, rs2)Operand Signedness RoleReturned 32-Bit Slice
Multiply (mul)0Any (S32 or U32)Shares low 32 bits across all modesBits 31..0
Multiply High (mulh)1S32×S32Signed by signed upper wordBits 63..32
Multiply High Signed-Unsigned (mulhsu)2S32×U32Signed by unsigned upper wordBits 63..32
Multiply High Unsigned (mulhu)3U32×U32Unsigned by unsigned upper wordBits 63..32

Evaluating rs1 equal to 0xFFFF_FFFF (−1 signed, 232−1 unsigned) and rs2 equal to 0x8000_0000 (−231 signed, +231 unsigned) shows all three modes sharing 0x8000_0000 in Bits 31..0 while diverging in Bits 63..32:

InstructionExact 64-Bit ProductFull 64-Bit Pattern
mulh(−1)(−231)=+2310x0000_0000_8000_0000
mulhsu(−1)(+231)=−2310xFFFF_FFFF_8000_0000
mulhu(232−1)(231)=263−2310x7FFF_FFFF_8000_0000
64-Bit Product Split: Shared Low 32 Bits (mul) vs. Divergent High 32 Bits
↔ Swipe horizontally to inspect all 64-bit product halves

Expanding every unsigned operand via U32(x)=S32(x)+x31⋅232 expresses both mixed (mulhsu) and unsigned (mulhu) products in terms of S32(a)⋅S32(b), isolating every sign-correction term with a factor of 232 so it alters only Bits 63..32:

S32(a)U32(b)=S32(a)S32(b)+232b31S32(a)U32(a)U32(b)=S32(a)S32(b)+232(a31S32(b)+b31S32(a)+a31b31232)

Because every 232-scaled correction vanishes modulo 232, all three signedness pairs produce the exact same low 32-bit pattern (Pmod232) for their 64-bit product P, holding both the unsigned and signed wrapped product via U32≡S32(mod232). The ISA therefore exposes only a single mul instruction for the low 32 bits across every signedness pair, while the differing correction terms above Bit 31 require three separate upper-half instructions (mulh, mulhsu, and mulhu).

To extract Bits 63..32 cleanly in oracle.py for any product P (rs1_s * rs2_s, rs1_s * rs2_u, or rs1_u * rs2_u), apply Section 4's right-shift bit decomposition at N=64 and k=32: splitting P=H⋅232+L (0≤L<232) identifies Bits 63..32 with H=⌊P/232⌋. Because Python's P >> 32 computes ⌊P/232⌋=H directly (even when P<0), wrapping u32(P >> 32) returns the exact upper 32-bit register pattern committed to rd by _set_reg whenever P stays inside its 64-bit word (keeping H inside one 32-bit word). Checking the extreme signed ([−231,231−1]) and unsigned ([0,232−1]) endpoint pairs confirms every product stays cleanly inside its 64-bit interval:

InstructionExact Product IntervalFits Within 64-Bit Range
mulhP∈[−262+231,262][−263,263−1]
mulhsuP∈[−263+231,(231−1)(232−1)][−263,263−1]
mulhuP∈[0,(232−1)2][0,264−1]

On the tightest signed boundary, mulhsu on 0x8000_0000 × 0xFFFF_FFFF evaluates (−231)(232−1)=−263+231, which rewrites as (−231)⋅232+231, fitting inside [−263,263−1] and returning upper half H=−231 (0x8000_0000).

Truncating Integer Division Semantics ​

RV32M completes integer arithmetic with four instructions pairing quotients and remainders across signed and unsigned operands: Divide (div), Divide Unsigned (divu), Remainder (rem), and Remainder Unsigned (remu). For positive integers, integer division is completely unambiguous: dividing 7 by 3 gives quotient q=2 and remainder r=1, satisfying a=q⋅b+r with 0≤r<b. When either operand is negative, however, the exact fraction −7/3≈−2.33 sits between −3 and −2, forcing every language and processor to pick a rounding direction. Python's // and % operators use floor division (⌊a/b⌋), rounding downward toward −∞ so -7 // 3 == -3 and -7 % 3 == +2 (matching the sign of divisor b). In contrast, C, hardware description languages such as SystemVerilog, and RISC-V use truncating division toward zero—keeping quotient magnitude symmetric around zero (-7 / 3 gives q=−2 and r=−1, rather than floor division's −3 as in Python // or the power-of-two arithmetic right shift from Right Shifts and Integer Floor Division).

The interactive number line below compares RISC-V truncation toward zero against Python floor division across all four dividend and divisor sign combinations.

Hardware Truncation Toward Zero vs. Python Floor Division
Number-Line Rounding Direction for -7 ÷ 3 (Exact Quotient ≈ -2.33)
↔ Swipe horizontally to inspect full number line
Takeaway: Exact quotient ≈ -2.33: hardware truncates right toward 0 (-2, rem -1), whereas Python floors left toward -∞ (-3, rem +2).

Writing the sign function sgn(x) piecewise makes the exact truncating quotient q and remainder r compact for every integer dividend a and nonzero divisor b≠0:

sgn(x)={+1if x>00if x=0−1if x<0q=sgn(a)sgn(b)⌊|a||b|⌋,r=a−qb

Why does rem always match the sign of dividend a (when non-zero) rather than divisor b? Dividing the non-negative magnitudes via ordinary positive division gives |a|=k|b|+r0 with k=⌊|a|/|b|⌋ and 0≤r0<|b|; multiplying both sides by sgn(a) and substituting |b|=sgn(b)b restores a directly:

a=sgn(a)(k|b|+r0)=sgn(a)sgn(b)kb+sgn(a)r0=qb+sgn(a)r0

Thus r=sgn(a)r0 automatically obeys |r|<|b| and inherits the sign of dividend a whenever r0>0—for −7/3, stepping q up by 1 from floor −3 to truncating −2 shifts the remainder down by b=3 from +2 to 2−3=−1.

All four RV32M division and remainder instructions share opcode 0x33 and funct7 0x01, dispatched by funct3 (4 through 7) across standard inputs and two special corner-case rules:

Instructionfunct3Standard Rule (rs2_u != 0, No Overflow)Divide by Zero (rs2_u == 0)Signed Overflow (INT32_MIN by −1)
div4Signed quotient truncated toward 0−1 (0xFFFF_FFFF)INT32_MIN (0x8000_0000)
divu5Unsigned quotient rs1_u // rs2_uUINT32_MAX (0xFFFF_FFFF)Not applicable
rem6Signed remainder (sign matches rs1_s if non-zero)rs1_s (original dividend)0
remu7Unsigned remainder rs1_u % rs2_urs1_u (original dividend)Not applicable

Two architectural rules explain those exact corner-case outputs without raising exceptions:

  1. Deterministic Divide-by-Zero Sentinels: Rather than raising an exception on rs2_u == 0, RISC-V defines fixed sentinel results (leaving compilers to emit an explicit branch check only when a source language requires a divide-by-zero trap). Returning the original dividend for rem/remu preserves q⋅0+a=a for any quotient q, while returning all-ones (0xFFFF_FFFF, reading as −1 signed and UINT32_MAX unsigned) lets div and divu share one divide-by-zero output pattern—and rem/remu share unmodified rs1—under one uniform fallback rule.
  2. Unique Signed Overflow (INT32_MIN divided by −1): Because signed 32-bit operands live in the discrete integer interval a,b∈[−231,231−1] (INT32_MIN to INT32_MAX, so |a|≤231), checking every nonzero divisor b≠0 shows why only one input pair overflows:
    • Whenever |b|≥2, the quotient magnitude |q|=⌊|a|/|b|⌋ is at most ⌊231/2⌋=230≤INT32_MAX.
    • When b=+1, q=a already sits inside [−231,231−1].
    • When b=−1 and a>−231, the smallest integer above −231 is −231+1, so |q|=|a|≤231−1=INT32_MAX fits cleanly (for example, 0x8000_0001 / -1 equals +231−1=INT32_MAX with remainder 0).
    • Only a=−231 (INT32_MIN) divided by b=−1 yields mathematical quotient +231=INT32_MAX+1, so div wraps +231 modulo 232 back to INT32_MIN (0x8000_0000) while rem returns 0, preserving −231≡(−231)(−1)+0(mod232).

Inside oracle.py, trunc_div_s32 evaluates abs(dividend) // abs(divisor) first and uses Python's boolean XOR ((dividend < 0) ^ (divisor < 0)) to negate q whenever exactly one operand is negative (producing -0 == 0 whenever q == 0, including dividend == 0 with divisor < 0). Oracle._exec_muldiv then dispatches div, divu, rem, and remu via selector constants F3_DIV through F3_REMU (verified across truncation, sign, near-extremal 0x8000_0001 / -1, overflow, and divide-by-zero boundaries in test_rv32m_division_truncation_overflow_and_div_by_zero):

py
def trunc_div_s32(dividend: int, divisor: int) -> int:
    """Divide signed 32-bit integers toward zero with non-trapping RISC-V corner semantics."""
    if divisor == 0:
        return -1
    if dividend == INT32_MIN and divisor == -1:
        return INT32_MIN
    # Truncate magnitude toward zero rather than Python's floor division (// toward -inf)
    q = abs(dividend) // abs(divisor)
    return -q if (dividend < 0) ^ (divisor < 0) else q

5. Memory Map and Bus Peripherals ​

General-purpose registers hold only 32 words at a time, so programs rely on addressable memory and peripheral devices connected to the CPU over shared address, data, and control wires (the hardware bus) to hold machine code, neural weights, call stacks, and device registers. Every bus transfer moves one of three standard widths: an 8-bit byte (1 byte), a 16-bit halfword (2 bytes), or a 32-bit word (4 bytes).

Load and Store Memory Instructions ​

To index into arrays, structs, and stack frames without extra add instructions, RISC-V load and store instructions add a sign-extended 12-bit constant offset directly to base register rs1 (offset(rs1)), reaching roughly ±2 KB (−2,048 to +2,047 bytes) around any pointer in one instruction. Eight memory instructions (I-type loads on opcode 0x03 and S-type stores on opcode 0x23) pair those base-plus-offset addresses with the three transfer widths and signed/unsigned extension rules (whose address-alignment bit checks we derive in Natural Alignment and Little-Endian Storage):

MnemonicDirection & Widthfunct3Required AlignmentRegister / Bus Extension Rule
Load Byte (lb) / Load Byte Unsigned (lbu)Load 1 byte0 / 4Any byte addressSign-extends (lb) or zero-extends (lbu) Bits 7..0 to 32 bits
Load Halfword (lh) / Load Halfword Unsigned (lhu)Load 2 bytes1 / 5Even (2-byte aligned)Sign-extends (lh) or zero-extends (lhu) Bits 15..0 to 32 bits
Load Word (lw)Load 4 bytes24-byte alignedCopies full 32-bit word into rd
Store Byte (sb)Store 1 byte0Any byte addressWrites low 8 bits (rs2 & 0xFF) to memory
Store Halfword (sh)Store 2 bytes1Even (2-byte aligned)Writes low 16 bits (rs2 & 0xFFFF) to memory
Store Word (sw)Store 4 bytes24-byte alignedWrites full 32-bit word rs2 to memory

Notice why only narrow loads (lb/lbu and lh/lhu) split by signedness: 32-bit lw performs no widening, and stores (sb, sh, sw of w∈{1,2,4} bytes) simply copy the low 8w bits identically for unsigned and signed integers (via U32≡S32(mod28w)), avoiding duplicate signed and unsigned store opcodes.

System-on-Chip Memory Map ​

Peripheral controllers attach their registers to fixed address ranges on the hardware bus in a design called Memory-Mapped Input/Output (MMIO), avoiding separate input/output opcodes for timers or serial ports. Combining the CPU core, local memory arrays, and MMIO peripherals inside one integrated design creates a complete System-on-Chip (SoC). On our brain SoC, four memory regions and seven 64 KB peripheral windows occupy disjoint ranges inside the 32-bit byte address space (0x0000_0000 through 0xFFFF_FFFF). Two primary peripheral blocks lead that window map: a timer and alarm unit (Core-Local Interruptor, or CLINT) and a serial console port (Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter, or UART). Startup instructions reside in permanent Read-Only Memory (ROM), while inner-loop neural weights live in fast on-chip scratchpad Block Random-Access Memory (BRAM). Larger program images reside in a soldered 4-wire external persistent flash chip (Quad Serial Peripheral Interface, or QSPI, flash). Fetching instructions directly from that flash chip without first copying code into BRAM is called Execute-In-Place (XIP). Finally, high-capacity external Synchronous Dynamic Random-Access Memory (SDRAM) supplies 32 MB for larger heaps and sensor and debug logs:

RegionByte Address RangeCapacityAccess RuleHardware Role
Boot ROM0x0000_0000–0x0000_3FFF16 KB (214)Read-OnlyPermanent startup ROM (BOOT_ROM_BASE)
BRAM0x1000_0000–0x1000_FFFF64 KB (216)Read / WriteFast internal BRAM (BRAM_BASE) for stack and weights
QSPI Flash0x2000_0000–0x20FF_FFFF16 MB (224)Read-OnlyExternal 4-wire XIP flash (QSPI_BASE)
SDRAM0x4000_0000–0x41FF_FFFF32 MB (225)Read / WriteExternal dynamic working memory (SDRAM_BASE) for heap and logs
CLINT0x8000_0000–0x8000_FFFF64 KB (216)32-bit MMIO64-bit monotonic timer and alarm unit (CLINT_BASE)
UART00x8001_0000–0x8001_FFFF64 KB (216)8/32-bit MMIOPrimary two-wire serial console (UART0_BASE)
MMIO Stubs0x8002_0000–0x8006_FFFFFive 64 KB blocks (216 each)Read / WriteReserved windows for sensor serial links, dual differential motor buses, camera trigger sync, and general-purpose digital pins (MMIO_STUB_BASE)

To inspect and drive memory from Python tests, Oracle provides load_bytes and load_words (internally passing bypass_ro=True to populate read-only code regions while rejecting MMIO windows). Calling reset clears CPU registers while keeping loaded program bytes intact, whereas any invalid CPU access triggers MemoryAccessFault inside bus_read or bus_write to raise a load or store access-fault trap (an abnormal control transfer to a handler, detailed in Section 6).

Power-of-Two Prefix Decoding ​

Aligning a power-of-two memory block to an exact multiple of its byte capacity gives every address inside that window the same upper bit prefix, eliminating subtractions and magnitude range checks. For example, every byte address inside 64 KB BRAM (0x1000_0000–0x1000_FFFF) begins with 0x1000, so address decoding detects a BRAM hit using only a 16-bit prefix equality check (addr >> 16) == 0x1000 while taking the low 16 bits directly as the offset inside BRAM. More generally, each SoC memory or peripheral window (treating the five MMIO stub blocks as individual 64 KB windows) uses a capacity 2K (1≤K<32) aligned to base address B=m⋅2K (m≥0, integer).

Splitting any byte address into its upper prefix and low K-bit offset turns an aligned memory range test into simple prefix equality for every window. For any 32-bit address a (addr) in [0,232−1] and aligned base B=m⋅2K (so m=B/2K=B≫K), substituting B and dividing by positive 2K turns the byte-window bounds into a normalized quotient interval:

B≤a<B+2K⟺m⋅2K≤a<(m+1)⋅2K⟺m≤a2K<m+1

Because m is an integer, m≤a/2K<m+1 holds if and only if ⌊a/2K⌋=m, and Section 4's unsigned right-shift floor identity ⌊a/2K⌋=a≫K equates the prefix slices directly:

⌊a2K⌋=m⟺(a≫K)=(B≫K)

Whenever ⌊a/2K⌋=m, Euclidean division gives a=m⋅2K+(amod2K)=B+(amod2K), so the window offset a−B=amod2K is simply the low K bits of addr with zero subtraction. Because B is an exact multiple of 2K, a full range test B≤a<B+2K collapses cleanly into comparing only the upper 32−K bits (Bits 31..K) via (addr >> K) == (B >> K).

Natural Alignment and Little-Endian Storage ​

Aligned 32-bit word memory accesses keep every 4-byte transfer inside one 4-byte slot rather than splitting words across two consecutive rows. Our CPU therefore enforces natural alignment: instruction fetches and word accesses (lw, sw) require addresses divisible by 4, while halfword accesses (lh, lhu, sh) require even addresses divisible by 2. For example, testing 4-byte word alignment inspects only the lowest two bits: 0x1000_0004 ends in binary 0b00 (0x1000_0004 & 3 == 0, aligned), whereas 0x1000_0005 ends in binary 0b01 (0x1000_0005 & 3 == 1, misaligned).

For any access width w=2k (k∈{0,1,2}), Euclidean division writes addr=q⋅2k+r (0≤r<2k) with remainder r=addr&(w−1) in the low k bits:

addr≡0(mod2k)⟺addr&(w−1)=0

Inside Oracle._exec_load and Oracle._exec_store, the oracle checks (addr & (width - 1)) != 0 before calling bus_read or bus_write. That ordering guarantees alignment traps preempt bus width or unmapped-address faults: targeting 32-bit-only CLINT (0x8000_0000) with odd halfword load lh x5, 1(x1) (x1 = 0x8000_0000) fails (addr & 1) != 0 first and raises a load-misaligned trap, whereas even lh x5, 0(x1) passes alignment and then triggers CLINT's MemoryAccessFault load-access fault.

All memory regions store multi-byte integers in little-endian byte order, placing Bits 7..0 at the lowest byte address and successively higher bytes at increasing addresses (0x1122_80FF at 0x1000_0000 stores 0xFF, 0x80, 0x22, 0x11). For any width w∈{1,2,4}, reassembling those w bytes gives val=∑i=0w−1mem[addr+i]⋅28i. Because SDRAM (32 MB) and QSPI flash (16 MB) span 48 MB combined, SparseMemory allocates 4,096-byte chunks lazily in _get_or_alloc_page on write_bytes and returns zero for untouched chunks in read_bytes:

py
    def read_bytes(self, addr: int, width: int) -> int:
        """Read `width` bytes (1, 2, or 4) from `addr` in little-endian byte order."""
        if width not in VALID_BUS_WIDTHS or not self.contains(addr, width):
            raise MemoryAccessFault(f"Out-of-bounds read at 0x{addr:08x} (width={width})")
        val = 0
        # Byte-by-byte loop handles multi-byte accesses crossing 4 KB chunk boundaries cleanly
        for i in range(width):
            offset = (addr + i) - self.base
            page = self._pages.get(offset // self.PAGE_SIZE)
            byte = page[offset % self.PAGE_SIZE] if page is not None else 0
            val |= byte << (8 * i)
        return val

Monotonic Timer and Serial Console ​

Autonomous control firmware relies on CLINT for deterministic timing and UART0 for ordered diagnostic byte streams whose bytes leave in arrival order (First-In, First-Out queues, or FIFOs). CLINT exposes a 64-bit monotonic tick counter (mtime) and alarm compare threshold (mtimecmp) over 32-bit bus registers, while UART0 exposes outgoing bytes (uart_tx_buf), incoming bytes (uart_rx_fifo), and a clock divider setting its serial bit rate (baud rate) without a shared clock wire (driven in Python tests via push_uart_rx and read_uart_tx, both cleared by reset). Inside oracle.py, _clint_offset, _clint_read, and _clint_write enforce 4-byte aligned 32-bit-only access across CLINT's four registers. Serial register validation in _uart_offset, _uart_read, and _uart_write permits 1- or 4-byte transfers on byte streams while enforcing 4-byte width on status and baud-divider words:
