Three quantitative hardware invariants explain the CLINT and UART0 design choices in oracle.py:

  1. 64-Bit Counter Lifetime and Rollover Tearing: On the brain board, a 50 MHz crystal oscillator (SYS_CLK_HZ = 50_000_000) ticks 50 million times per second, so a 32-bit counter wraps in seconds while a 64-bit counter (converting at 86,400 seconds per day and 365.25 days per year) never rolls over in service:

    T32=23250×106 Hz≈85.899 sT64=26450 MHz×86,400 s/d×365.25 d/yr≈11,691 years

    Because a 32-bit bus reads mtime in two separate instructions, a carry tick landing between the low-word and high-word reads stitches halves from different ticks into a bogus timestamp (rollover tear hazard). Firmware eliminates tearing with a 3-read tear-free retry loop (hi1 from CLINT_MTIME_HI, lo from CLINT_MTIME_LO, and hi2 from CLINT_MTIME_HI, retrying while hi1 != hi2, verified at the 32-bit carry boundary in test_counter_carry_and_64bit_rollover):

    64-Bit Timer Rollover Tear Hazard vs. 3-Read Retry Loop
    ↔ Swipe horizontally to inspect the 64-bit rollover timeline

    Because mtime increments monotonically and takes 264 ticks (about 11,691 years) to wrap CLINT_MTIME_HI back to its starting value, hi1 == hi2 guarantees zero carries occurred between those two reads, and the 85.9-second spacing between carries bounds retries to at most one extra pass.

  2. Glitch-Free 3-Store Alarm Updates: CLINT compares the two 64-bit registers continuously and asserts an alarm signal whenever mtime >= mtimecmp (mtimecmp resets to UINT64_MAX, 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF, so alarms never fire before firmware arms them). Because a 32-bit CPU cannot update both halves of mtimecmp in one store, either naive 2-store order briefly exposes a hybrid threshold that can dip to or below mtime and fire a false alarm—even when both the old and new 64-bit thresholds sit safely in the future. With mtime at 0x0000_0001_8000_0000, both naive orders briefly expose the exact same false-alarm hybrid 0x0000_0001_0000_0010 <= mtime:

    Naive OrderOld → New mtimecmpFirst StoreExposed Hybrid (≤mtime)
    HI First (pulling earlier)0x0000_0002_0000_0010 → 0x0000_0001_C000_00000x0000_0001 to CLINT_MTIMECMP_HI0x0000_0001_0000_0010
    LO First (raising across carry)0x0000_0001_C000_0000 → 0x0000_0002_0000_00100x0000_0010 to CLINT_MTIMECMP_LO0x0000_0001_0000_0010

    Split any future thresholds Told>mtime and Tnew>mtime into their upper and lower 32-bit halves (oldhi, oldlo) and (newhi, newlo). Executing three stores in order—first 0xFFFF_FFFF to CLINT_MTIMECMP_LO, second newhi to CLINT_MTIMECMP_HI, and third newlo to CLINT_MTIMECMP_LO—pushes the low half to its maximum before swapping the high word so both intermediate 64-bit thresholds stay strictly above mtime:

    T1=(oldhi≪32)∣0xFFFF_FFFF≥Told>mtimeT2=(newhi≪32)∣0xFFFF_FFFF≥Tnew>mtime

    Tracing that exact earlier-alarm update (mtime = 0x0000_0001_8000_0000, 0x0000_0002_0000_0010 to 0x0000_0001_C000_0000) confirms zero spurious alarms across all three stores:

    Store StepTarget RegisterWritten WordResulting 64-Bit mtimecmpRelation to mtime
    1CLINT_MTIMECMP_LO0xFFFF_FFFF0x0000_0002_FFFF_FFFFStrictly above mtime (T1>mtime)
    2CLINT_MTIMECMP_HI0x0000_00010x0000_0001_FFFF_FFFFStrictly above mtime (T2>mtime)
    3CLINT_MTIMECMP_LO0xC000_00000x0000_0001_C000_0000Reaches final target (Tnew>mtime)

  3. UART Baud Quantization Drift: Without a shared clock wire, a UART transmitter wraps each 8-bit byte inside a 10-bit frame (1 start bit, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit); the receiver synchronizes on the start edge and samples the center of every bit cell, succeeding as long as cumulative timing drift stays within ±0.5 bit-periods (±50%).

    At SYS_CLK_HZ = 50_000_000 and 115,200 baud, dividing 50,000,000 by 115,200 yields exact divider period 15,625/36 (≈434.0278) ticks per serial bit, so rounding to default integer divider self.uart_bauddiv (434, stored in UART0_BAUDDIV) introduces per-bit relative timing error:

    ϵ=434−15,6253615,62536=−115,625=−0.0064%

    Across all 10 bits of a frame, cumulative phase drift reaches only 10|ϵ|=0.064%—nearly three orders of magnitude inside the ±50% half-bit sampling window.

6. Control Flow and Trap Handling ​

In straight-line execution, self.pc advances by 4 bytes after every 32-bit instruction. Execution departs from sequential pc + 4 flow in two ways: explicit control-flow instructions (conditional branches and subroutine jumps) and traps, which split into synchronous exceptions (deterministic faults or firmware calls caused by the active instruction) and asynchronous interrupts (external, software, or timer Interrupt Requests, or IRQs, that preempt execution between instructions).

Conditional Branches and Subroutine Jumps ​

Every non-trivial robot controller needs conditional if/else choices, counting loops, direct subroutine calls, and jump tables through function pointers. RISC-V splits explicit control-flow transfers cleanly into two groups: six conditional B-type branches compare two registers and jump when the relation holds, while two unconditional jump instructions save return link address cur_pc + 4 in rd (conventionally x1, the subroutine return-link register) so subroutines can return cleanly. In oracle.py, Oracle._exec_branch handles conditional branches (opcode 0x63 with decoded 13-bit B-type signed offset imm13), _exec_jal (opcode 0x6F with decoded 21-bit J-type signed offset imm21) handles direct jumps, and _exec_jalr (opcode 0x67 with decoded 12-bit I-type signed offset imm12) handles indirect jumps:

MnemonicFormat / funct3Branch / Jump Condition and TargetLink Writeback and Alignment Rule
Branch if Equal (beq)B-type / 0Jump to u32(cur_pc + imm13) if rs1_u == rs2_uTraps with an instruction-misaligned fault if taken and (target & 3) != 0
Branch if Not Equal (bne)B-type / 1Jump to u32(cur_pc + imm13) if rs1_u != rs2_uUntaken branches advance to cur_pc + 4 without checking target alignment
Branch if Less Than (blt)B-type / 4Jump to u32(cur_pc + imm13) if rs1_s < rs2_sSigned 32-bit comparison; alignment checked only if taken
Branch Greater or Equal (bge)B-type / 5Jump to u32(cur_pc + imm13) if rs1_s >= rs2_sSigned 32-bit comparison; alignment checked only if taken
Branch Less Than Unsigned (bltu)B-type / 6Jump to u32(cur_pc + imm13) if rs1_u < rs2_uUnsigned 32-bit comparison; alignment checked only if taken
Branch Greater or Equal Unsigned (bgeu)B-type / 7Jump to u32(cur_pc + imm13) if rs1_u >= rs2_uUnsigned 32-bit comparison; alignment checked only if taken
Jump and Link (jal)J-type / noneUnconditional u32(cur_pc + imm21)Saves cur_pc + 4 to rd; traps before writeback if (target & 3) != 0
Jump and Link Register (jalr)I-type / 0u32((rs1_u + imm12) & JALR_TARGET_MASK) (0xFFFF_FFFE)Sign-extends imm12, clears Bit 0 first, checks (target & 3) != 0, and captures (latches) rs1_u before saving cur_pc + 4

RISC-V defines jalr to clear Bit 0 (JALR_TARGET_MASK = 0xFFFF_FFFE) before checking alignment so function pointers can carry a 1-bit metadata tag in their least-significant bit and stay compatible with optional 16-bit compressed instructions, while 32-bit-only cores like ours still trap whenever Bit 1 remains set. Because jalr also captures (latches) rs1_u before writing rd, self-overwriting calls behave deterministically across both alignment outcomes (verified in test_jalr_bit0_snap_and_untaken_misaligned_branch). Starting from cur_pc equal to 0x0000_0000 and x2 equal to 0x1000_0000, jalr x2, 1(x2) clears Bit 0 to snap (0x1000_0000 + 1) & 0xFFFF_FFFE cleanly onto 0x1000_0000 while writing link address 0x0000_0004 into x2. In contrast, jalr x2, 2(x2) from that same state leaves Bit 1 set at 0x1000_0002, trapping before writeback so x2 remains untouched at 0x1000_0000.

Wiring x0 into beq, jal, and jalr provides standard control pseudoinstructions without extra opcodes, while swapping rs1 and rs2 in the six B-type branches covers all ten signed and unsigned relational comparisons:

PseudoinstructionMachine EncodingAlgebraic / Control Equivalence
Branch if Equal to Zero (beqz rs1, off)beq rs1, x0, offBranches when rs1 == 0
Branch if Greater Than (bgt rs1, rs2, off)blt rs2, rs1, offCommutes operands: a>b⟺b<a
Branch if Less or Equal (ble rs1, rs2, off)bge rs2, rs1, offCommutes operands: a≤b⟺b≥a
Unconditional Jump (j off)jal x0, offUnconditional jump discarding return link into x0
Return from Subroutine (ret)jalr x0, 0(x1)Returns to link register x1 without saving a new link

Why do six branch instructions suffice for all ten comparisons (=, ≠, <, ≥, >, ≤ across signed and unsigned)? Equality and inequality (= and ≠, handled by beq and bne) are identical for signed and unsigned operands per Section 4's equality invariance, leaving two shared equality relations plus eight ordered inequalities (<, ≥, >, ≤ in signed and unsigned variants)—ten distinct comparisons in total. Operand commutation (a>b⟺b<a and a≤b⟺b≥a) maps the four > and ≤ relations onto the four base < and ≥ instructions (blt, bge, bltu, bgeu) by swapping rs1 and rs2 in the assembler or compiler, so 2+4=6 branch instructions suffice.

Control Registers and System Instructions ​

To configure interrupt masks, trap vector addresses, and cycle counters without consuming x0–x31, each processor core (hardware thread, or hart) provides a dedicated bank of 32-bit Control and Status Registers (CSRs). The RISC-V Zicsr extension organizes those registers into a 12-bit address space (0x000–0xFFF, 4,096 slots). Our single-core CPU runs permanently in Machine privilege mode (M-mode, binary 0b11), the highest RISC-V privilege level with direct access to physical memory and control registers. Most writable CSR fields silently mask unsupported bits rather than faulting, a convention called Write Any Values, Reads Legal Values (WARL). In contrast, writes to read-only CSRs (misa and the static identification registers) raise an illegal-instruction trap in _write_csr (paired with reads in _read_csr):

CSR AddressRegisterAccess and WARL MaskingArchitectural Role
0x300mstatusWARL: Interrupt Enable (Bit 3) and Previous Interrupt Enable (Bit 7) writable; Previous Privilege (Bits 12..11) fixed 0b11Machine Status: global interrupt switch and saved trap state
0x301misaRead-Only 0x4080_1100; writes trapMachine ISA: reports 32-bit base plus I (integer), M (multiply/divide), and X (custom) extensions
0x304mieWARL: Software (Bit 3), Timer (Bit 7), and External (Bit 11) writableMachine Interrupt Enable: per-channel interrupt masks
0x305mtvecWARL: Bits 31..2 base; Bits 1..0 snaps modes >1 to 0Machine Trap Vector: handler base and dispatch mode (0 Direct, 1 Vectored)
0x340mscratchFull 32-bit Read / WriteMachine Scratch: dedicated word for trap handlers to swap a stack pointer
0x341mepcWARL: clears Bits 1..0 (val & 0xFFFF_FFFC)Machine Exception PC: saved resume address across traps
0x342mcauseFull 32-bit Read / WriteMachine Trap Cause: Bit 31 (1 interrupt / 0 exception) + cause code
0x343mtvalFull 32-bit Read / WriteMachine Trap Value: offending address or raw instruction word
0x344mipSoftware (Bit 3) and External (Bit 11) writable; Timer (Bit 7) live wireMachine Interrupt Pending: software/external latches and mtime >= mtimecmp
0xB00 / 0xB80mcycle / mcyclehTwo 32-bit Read / Write halves (low / high)Machine Cycle Counter: 64-bit counter incrementing on every step (instructions and traps)
0xB02 / 0xB82minstret / minstrethTwo 32-bit Read / Write halves (low / high)Machine Instructions Retired: 64-bit counter for completed non-trapping instructions
0xF11–0xF14mvendorid, marchid, mimpid, mhartidRead-Only zero; writes trapStatic vendor, architecture, implementation, and core (0) IDs

Inside mstatus, the global Machine Interrupt Enable (MIE, Bit 3) switch gates all interrupts. Hardware preserves prior state across trap entry and return in Machine Previous Interrupt Enable (MPIE, Bit 7) and fixed Machine Previous Privilege (MPP, Bits 12..11 equal to 0b11). Meanwhile, read-only Machine ISA (misa) returns 0x4080_1100: Bits 31..30 equal 0b01 for 32-bit width, Bit 8 encodes base integer extension I, Bit 12 encodes multiply/divide extension M, and Bit 23 indicates custom extensions X.

Notice how mie and Machine Interrupt Pending (mip) align every interrupt source onto the exact same bit column so hardware evaluates all enabled requests in one bitwise AND (self._live_mip() & self.mie):

Interrupt ChannelBit Indexmie Mask Bitmip Pending BitTrigger Source
SoftwareBit 3Machine Software Interrupt Enable (MSIE)Machine Software Interrupt Pending (MSIP)Software write to mip Bit 3
TimerBit 7Machine Timer Interrupt Enable (MTIE)Machine Timer Interrupt Pending (MTIP)Live wire mtime >= mtimecmp
ExternalBit 11Machine External Interrupt Enable (MEIE)Machine External Interrupt Pending (MEIP)External peripheral interrupt line

Splitting a control-register update across separate read, modify, and write instructions breaks whenever an interrupt fires mid-sequence and modifies the same CSR, because the resuming write silently overwrites the handler's update. To eliminate that race, Oracle._exec_zicsr fuses read and update into six indivisible (atomic) Zicsr instructions (opcode 0x73) performing Read and Write (csrrw), Read and Set (csrrs), and Read and Clear (csrrc) on csr_addr (Bits 31..20). Their immediate counterparts (csrrwi, csrrsi, csrrci) replace register operand rs1_u with a zero-extended 5-bit unsigned immediate (uimm, stored in Bits 19..15), where src denotes whichever source value (rs1_u or uimm) supplies the update:

Mnemonicfunct3Atomic Operation (Reads old, Writes New Value)Write Suppression Rule
csrrw / csrrwi1 / 5Atomically writes src to csr and returns old into rd (leaving rd untouched on trap)Never suppressed (always attempts the CSR write; csrrw x0, misa, x0 traps)
csrrs / csrrsi2 / 6Atomically writes old | src to csr and returns old into rd (leaving rd untouched on trap)Writes only if source field rs1 (or 5-bit uimm) is non-zero (csrr rd, csr aliases csrrs rd, csr, x0 to read safely)
csrrc / csrrci3 / 7Atomically clears every bit set to 1 in src (32-bit old & ~src) and returns old into rd (leaving rd untouched on trap)Writes only if source field rs1 (or 5-bit uimm) is non-zero

Inside _exec_zicsr, funct3 factors cleanly by bit position: Bit 2 (ZICSR_IMM_BIT, funct3 5–7 vs. 1–3) selects the immediate variant, while Bits 1..0 (ZICSR_OP_MASK) select rw (1), rs (2), or rc (3). Because uimm occupies the exact same Bits 19..15 slice as rs1, the method reuses the 5-bit integer rs1 directly as src_val and checks rs1 != 0 uniformly for both rs1 == x0 and uimm == 0 write suppression. For bit-clear (rc), XORing src_val with all-ones MASK32 flips Bits 31..0 as an unsigned 32-bit NOT without producing Python's negative ~src_val. Finally, wrote_minstret suppresses the normal retirement +1 whenever an explicit CSR write targets minstret or minstreth, because minstret increments at retirement after CSR execution (whereas mcycle increments before execution and is overwritten directly by a CSR write):

py
        src_val = rs1 if (funct3 & ZICSR_IMM_BIT) else rs1_u
        op = funct3 & ZICSR_OP_MASK
        if op == ZICSR_OP_RW:     # csrrw / csrrwi always attempt a CSR write
            new_val, do_write = src_val, True
        elif op == ZICSR_OP_RS:   # csrrs / csrrsi skip write when rs1 == 0 (read-only query)
            new_val, do_write = old_val | src_val, (rs1 != 0)
        else:                     # csrrc / csrrci clear bits via MASK32 XOR; skip if rs1 == 0
            new_val, do_write = old_val & (MASK32 ^ src_val), (rs1 != 0)

        wrote_minstret = False
        if do_write:
            # Trap before writing rd so faulted read-only CSR writes leave rd untouched;
            # rs1_u was latched before writeback so rd == rs1 swaps remain atomic.
            if not self._write_csr(csr_addr, new_val):
                return self._trap_trace(cur_pc, insn, CAUSE_ILLEGAL_INSN, insn)
            wrote_minstret = csr_addr in (CSR_MINSTRET, CSR_MINSTRETH)

InstructionOpcode / EncodingArchitectural Effect
Environment Call (ecall)0x0000_0073 (opcode 0x73)Raises synchronous request trap (mcause equals 11 in M-mode)

Trap Entry and Return Choreography ​

Whenever an enabled asynchronous interrupt or synchronous exception fires, hardware switches into the trap handler atomically without modifying any general-purpose register x1–x31. In one step, the processor saves the word-aligned resume address into mepc (alongside mcause and mtval), copies global MIE into MPIE while clearing MIE to 0 to shield the handler from nested preemption, and jumps pc to the handler address encoded in mtvec. After the handler services the interrupt source (or advances mepc past a synchronous trap such as ecall), executing mret restores MIE from MPIE and resumes normal execution at mepc.

In oracle.py, Oracle._check_pending_interrupt runs before every instruction fetch to check whether global MIE equals 1 and any enabled request in self._live_mip() & self.mie is active, arbitrating external ahead of software ahead of timer. Whether triggered by a pre-fetch interrupt or a synchronous exception, Oracle._take_trap executes that atomic transition—clearing the low two address bits with WORD_ALIGN_MASK (0xFFFF_FFFC) and extracting the lower 31-bit trap number (code) from mcause with MCAUSE_CODE_MASK (0x7FFF_FFFF). When mtvec selects Direct dispatch (mode == 0), every trap jumps to base; when mtvec selects Vectored dispatch (mode == 1), synchronous exceptions still enter at base whereas asynchronous interrupts index into a contiguous jump table of 4-byte instruction slots starting at base, entering at u32(base + 4 * code):

py
    def _take_trap(self, cause: int, tval: int, is_interrupt: bool) -> int:
        """Execute atomic hardware trap entry: save context, disable interrupts, jump to `mtvec`."""
        # 1. 4-byte instruction alignment forces mepc Bits 1..0 = 0; mtval keeps exact faulting PC
        self.mepc = self.pc & WORD_ALIGN_MASK
        self.mcause = u32(cause)
        self.mtval = u32(tval)

        # 2. Push current MIE -> MPIE and mask MIE = 0 atomically
        self._set_mstatus_irq_bits(mie=False, mpie=bool(self.mstatus & MSTATUS_MIE_BIT))

        # 3. Dispatch to Direct base or Vectored (base + 4 * cause_code) handler address
        base = self.mtvec & WORD_ALIGN_MASK
        mode = self.mtvec & MTVEC_MODE_MASK
        if is_interrupt and mode == MTVEC_MODE_VECTORED:
            target = u32(base + INSN_SIZE_BYTES * (cause & MCAUSE_CODE_MASK))
        else:
            target = base
        self.pc = target
        return target

Writing trap entry and mret as explicit state-transition equations over (pc,mepc,MIE,MPIE)—alongside the rule that hardware leaves all 31 general-purpose registers x1–x31 untouched—clarifies both resumption and interrupt stack bootstrapping. Here primed symbols (pc′, mepc′, MIE′, MPIE′, mcause′) denote post-transition state values immediately after trap entry or mret:

  • irq∈{0,1} is Bit 31 of mcause′ (1 for asynchronous interrupts, 0 for synchronous exceptions).
  • base=mtvec&0xFFFF_FFFC (WORD_ALIGN_MASK) and mode=mtvec&3.
  • code=mcause′&0x7FFF_FFFF (MCAUSE_CODE_MASK).
  • Indicator I[cond] evaluates to 1 if cond holds and 0 otherwise.

For trap entry:

mepc′=pc&0xFFFF_FFFCMPIE′=MIE,MIE′=0pc′=(base+4⋅I[irq=1∧mode=1]⋅code)mod232

For trap return (mret):

MIE′=MPIE,MPIE′=1pc′=mepc&0xFFFF_FFFC

Written mtvecStored mtvec (WARL)Trap Event (mcause)Saved StateNext pc'
0x1000_01030x1000_0100 (Direct, mode 0)Timer IRQ 7 (0x8000_0007)mepc = 0x0000_0020, MPIE = 1, MIE = 00x1000_0100

Three architectural consequences follow from these state-transition equations together with hardware leaving x1–x31 untouched:

  1. Atomic Interrupt Masking and Restore: Clearing MIE to zero after copying it into MPIE shields the handler (Interrupt Service Routine, or ISR) from re-entrant preemption while saving registers, and mret atomically restores MIE to its prior value (1 when interrupting normal execution) upon return.
  2. Exact Resume Offset: Because an asynchronous interrupt preempted the instruction at mepc before it ran, the ISR clears the IRQ source (for example, advancing mtimecmp) and executes mret with mepc unchanged, whereas a synchronous ecall or ebreak handler advances mepc to mepc + 4 so mret resumes at the next instruction instead of repeating the trap.
  3. Zero-Clobber mscratch Bootstrap: When an asynchronous timer or external interrupt fires, all 31 writable registers x1–x31 hold live interrupted program state, so an ISR cannot even execute lui/addi to load a stack pointer (conventionally x2) without overwriting a live register. Executing the single atomic swap csrrw x2, mscratch, x2 saves the interrupted program's stack pointer x2 into mscratch while loading the dedicated ISR stack pointer from mscratch into x2 in the exact same instruction—freeing x2 to push the remaining registers onto the ISR stack with zero register loss.

7. Custom Neural Multiply-Accumulate Extension ​

Running real-time neural inference on an embedded robot control loop reduces mathematically to dense matrix-vector multiplication and vector dot products plus a constant per-neuron offset (bias) of the form c+∑jajbj. Computing one element of that sum with base integer instructions (lw, lh, mul, add, and conditional overflow-clamping branches blt/bge) requires roughly six to eight instructions per weight—plus loop-counter updates and branch overhead. Doubling throughput while eliminating inner-loop overflow branches frees real-time processor budget for sensor filtering and motor safety checks.

Our brain robot controller solves a concrete instance of this workload inside a 50 Hz (20 ms period) quadruped walking policy. The controller feeds a 48-element sensor state vector (joint angles, velocities, body orientation, and gait clock phase) through a compact neural network (Multi-Layer Perceptron, or MLP) with layer widths 48, 128, 128, and 12 motor targets, holding 48×128+128×128+128×12=24,064 signed 16-bit weights (47.0 KB, fitting completely inside the 64 KB on-chip BRAM introduced in Section 5). The brain CPU is implemented as a softcore processor, meaning its logic blocks and wiring are configured onto a reprogrammable Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) chip rather than etched into fixed custom silicon. Preventing actuator-torque sign inversions and fitting within two physical limits of that reprogrammable chip together shape our custom neural instructions.

Saturating Clamping and Dual-Lane Datapath ​

In general modular arithmetic, overflowing a signed 32-bit sum wraps silently from +2,147,483,647 to −2,147,483,648, which would command a robot joint actuator at full reverse torque instead of full forward torque. Control datapaths prevent violent sign inversions using saturating arithmetic, clamping any sum falling outside [INT32_MIN,INT32_MAX] cleanly to the nearest endpoint via sat32:

py
def sat32(val: int) -> int:
    """Clamp an integer to signed 32-bit bounds [INT32_MIN, INT32_MAX] without wrapping."""
    if val < INT32_MIN:
        return INT32_MIN
    if val > INT32_MAX:
        return INT32_MAX
    return val

Two physical limits on the target FPGA chip shape our custom instruction encoding (opcode 0x0B):

  1. Register-File Port Limit: Programmable logic blocks inside our FPGA implement a two-read, one-write (2R1W) general-purpose register file efficiently, whereas feeding a running accumulator alongside two source operand registers (rs1, rs2) would demand three simultaneous register reads (3R1W). Keeping a dedicated 32-bit signed architectural accumulator (self.mac_acc) alongside x0–x31 supplies the third operand internally inside Oracle with zero extra register-file ports.
  2. Hardwired 18-Bit Multiplier Blocks: Embedded FPGA dedicated arithmetic blocks (Digital Signal Processing slices, or DSP slices) contain hardwired 18×18-bit signed multipliers, making two parallel 16-bit signed lanes packed inside one 32-bit register nearly free alongside existing 32-bit multiplier hardware. Packing lower halfword Bits 15..0 (a0, b0) and upper halfword Bits 31..16 (a1, b1) into rs1 and rs2 delivers two signed 16-bit multiply-accumulates in a single instruction (Single Instruction, Multiple Data, or SIMD), sign-extending each 16-bit lane via s16:
py
def s16(val: int) -> int:
    """Interpret lower 16 bits as signed two's complement: S_16(b) = U_16(b) - b_15 * 2^16."""
    return sign_extend(val, 16)

First-Step Accumulator Overflow Bounds ​

Because mac.clr starts each dot product from a cleared accumulator (base_acc = 0), a natural hardware question is whether the saturation clamp can ever be bypassed on that first step. Starting from zero can still saturate positively on the very first step for one unique extremal input pair, whereas no input pair can saturate negatively:

Input Pair (rs1, rs2)Exact Sum of Lane ProductsSaturation Outcome
0x8000_8000, 0x8000_8000(−32,768)2+(−32,768)2=+231Clamps (INT32_MAX+1→INT32_MAX)
0x8000_8000, 0x7FFF_7FFF2(−32,768)(+32,767)=−231+65,536Stays strictly inside (>INT32_MIN)

Because every unpacked signed 16-bit lane lives in the discrete integer interval [−215,215−1], each lane product pi=aibi (i∈{0,1}) obeys:

−230+215=(−215)(215−1)≤pi≤(−215)2=+230

Summing both lanes gives the two-lane extrema Smin and Smax:

Smin=−231+216>INT32_MINSmax=+231=INT32_MAX+1

Those bounds immediately establish both asymmetry properties:

  1. No First-Step Negative Saturation: Smin=−231+65,536 sits 65,536 above INT32_MIN, so mac.clr can never clamp negatively in one instruction.

  2. Unique First-Step Positive Saturation: Whenever lane i avoids (−215,−215), any negative-by-negative pair has at least one integer factor ≥−215+1, any positive-by-positive pair peaks at (215−1)2=230−216+1, and any opposite-sign or zero pair gives pi≤0:

    pi≤(−215)(−215+1)=230−215p0+p1≤(230−215)+230=231−215<INT32_MAX

    Thus sat32 clamps to INT32_MAX (0x7FFF_FFFF) on step one if and only if all four halfwords equal −215 (0x8000_8000 paired with 0x8000_8000).

Across multi-step dot products, clamping after every mac instruction via sat32 also makes accumulation order-sensitive whenever an intermediate peak crosses INT32_MAX. Starting from mac_acc = INT32_MAX - 255 (0x7FFF_FF00) with term A adding +500 (50⋅10) and term B adding −400 (−40⋅10), reversing those two instructions yields two distinct final values:

  • Positive Peak First (A then B): Adding +500 clamps INT32_MAX + 245 down to INT32_MAX (discarding 245 units of positive overshoot), so adding −400 finishes at INT32_MAX - 400.
  • Negative Offset First (B then A): Adding −400 dips cleanly to INT32_MAX - 655, keeping the subsequent +500 unclamped at exact total INT32_MAX - 155.

8. Unified Decoding and Lockstep Verification ​

With every instruction family, memory window, trap priority, and custom neural instruction specified, we must now close Section 1's verification contract before writing any hardware circuit code. That verification contract rests on two pillars: confirming that every possible 32-bit machine word decodes deterministically without ambiguity, and bounding per-step comparison work so hardware circuit simulation matches our Python oracle in constant work per step.

Unified 32-Bit Instruction Decoder ​

Every machine word fetched by the brain CPU maps onto one of twelve disjoint 7-bit primary opcode values—all ending in 0b11—or falls immediately into CAUSE_ILLEGAL_INSN = 2. Because those twelve primary opcodes and the unassigned-opcode trap class partition the 7-bit opcode space (0x00..0x7F) without overlap, and secondary selectors (funct3, funct7, 12-bit CSR addresses with write-enable rs1 checks, or full 32-bit system constants) partition each major group disjointly, every 32-bit integer word has a single unique decoding across all 232 bit patterns. That disjoint partition guarantees a deterministic contract: every 32-bit word maps to at most one operation or the default illegal-instruction trap—with zero overlapping encodings or priority ambiguities—while reusing standard R-Type register-index fields directly for custom Xapex (0x0B). The table below partitions all twelve primary opcode groups, their secondary selectors, and every unassigned or illegal pattern routed to CAUSE_ILLEGAL_INSN:

Primary opcodeFormat & GroupSecondary Partition RuleUnassigned / Illegal Patterns
0x03I-Type Loadsfunct3 in {0, 1, 2, 4, 5} (lb, lh, lw, lbu, lhu)funct3 in {3, 6, 7} traps (mcause 2)
0x0BR-Type Xapexfunct7 == 0x00 and funct3 in {0, 1, 2, 3}Any other funct7 or funct3 >= 4 traps
0x0FI-Type Orderingfunct3 in {0, 1} (fence, fence.i)funct3 >= 2 traps
0x13I-Type Integerfunct3 in {0, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7}; shifts 1 (0x00) and 5 (0x00/0x20)funct3 == 1 traps for funct7 != 0x00; funct3 == 5 traps for funct7 outside {0x00, 0x20}
0x17U-Type PC OffsetUnique auipc encoding (no funct3/funct7)None (all upper 25 bits legal)
0x23S-Type Storesfunct3 in {0, 1, 2} (sb, sh, sw)funct3 >= 3 traps
0x33R-Type Integer / RV32Mfunct7 == 0x00 (all 8 funct3), 0x01 (all 8 RV32M), 0x20 (funct3 0 or 5)Any other funct7 or 0x20 sub-code traps
0x37U-Type Upper LoadUnique lui encoding (no funct3/funct7)None (all upper 25 bits legal)
0x63B-Type Branchesfunct3 in {0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 7} (beq..bgeu)funct3 in {2, 3} traps
0x67I-Type Indirect Jumpfunct3 == 0 (jalr)funct3 != 0 traps
0x6FJ-Type Direct JumpUnique jal encoding (no funct3/funct7)None (all upper 25 bits legal)
0x73I-Type System / CSRfunct3 == 0 exact ecall/ebreak/mret/wfi; funct3 in {1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7} valid CSRPrivileged encodings (funct3 == 0 outside those four words), funct3 == 4, unimplemented CSR addresses, or read-only CSR writes trap

Deterministic Fetch and Retirement Priority ​

Real processors interact continuously with live peripheral wires such as timer alarms and external serial interrupts, so a single clock tick can face competing events at the exact same instant. If hardware and our golden model disagreed on whether to increment timers before checking interrupts or whether a misaligned pc fails before reading memory, lockstep verification would fail immediately on subtle timing boundaries. Oracle.step() wraps 64-bit counters modulo 264 with MASK64 (0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF), runs one fixed sequence of pre-fetch checks, and always returns a 10-field StepTrace commit receipt summarizing the step's observable state delta. The opening slice of step() below shows the pre-fetch clock advance, pending-interrupt preemption check, and instruction fetch:

py
        cur_pc = self.pc
        # 1. Advance free-running 64-bit clocks pre-fetch (wrapped to 64 bits) so alarms fire
        self.mcycle = (self.mcycle + 1) & MASK64
        self.mtime = (self.mtime + 1) & MASK64
        if (irq_trace := self._check_pending_interrupt(cur_pc)) is not None:
            return irq_trace

        # 2. Fetch aligned 32-bit instruction word at cur_pc
        fetched = self._fetch_instruction(cur_pc)
        if isinstance(fetched, StepTrace):
            return fetched
        insn = fetched

Five strict ordering guarantees govern every clock tick inside step():

  1. Pre-Fetch Clock Advance: mcycle and mtime increment modulo 264 (MASK64) before checking pending interrupts so a timer deadline expiring on cycle k triggers preemption immediately on step k (mcycle counts every step, trapping or retiring).
  2. Pre-Fetch Interrupt Priority: Enabled external, software, and timer interrupts preempt cur_pc before instruction fetch runs, guaranteeing zero speculative memory reads when an interrupt fires.
  3. Instruction-Fetch Alignment and Access Check: _fetch_instruction checks 4-byte cur_pc alignment before reading the bus and returns an early fetch-fault StepTrace on misalignment or unmapped/MMIO access before decode or operand latching runs.
  4. Fault-Checked Operand Latching and Dispatch: Unsigned 32-bit source register reads (rs1_u, rs2_u from self.regs[rs1] and self.regs[rs2]) latch prior values before writeback, and dispatch helpers validate instruction legality, alignment, bus bounds, and CSR write permissions before executing any validated store, CSR, mstatus, or mac_acc mutation—returning either an early StepTrace trap receipt or a pending non-trapping ExecOutcome commit record (including suppress_minstret for explicit minstret/minstreth writes).
  5. Atomic Retirement Commit: Only non-trapping instructions reach commit, applying hardwired x0 protection via _set_reg, updating self.pc, and incrementing minstret unless suppress_minstret preserves an explicit Zicsr write targeting minstret or minstreth. Because every step increments mcycle modulo 264 while only non-trapping retirements increment minstret, (mcycle−minstret)mod264 equals the cumulative trap count modulo 264 whenever execution starts from reset (mcycle = minstret = 0) and software leaves mcycle/mcycleh and minstret/minstreth untouched.

Precise Faults and Inductive Trace Equivalence ​

Comparing every bit of state across 32 general-purpose registers, control registers, and 48 MB of memory after each executed instruction would require millions of comparisons per step. Instead, Oracle.step() normalizes every numeric commit delta as an unsigned 32-bit integer inside the 10-field StepTrace record (alongside optional int | None fields and boolean flags):

py
@dataclass
class StepTrace:
    """Record of one step executed by `Oracle.step()`.

    All integer address, word, and register fields (`pc`, `insn`, `next_pc`, `rd_val`,
    `mem_addr`, `mem_val`, and `trap_cause`) hold unsigned 32-bit values in [0, 2^32 - 1]
    (sub-word stores mask `mem_val` to 8/16 bits; signed loads sign-extend `mem_val` via
    `u32`). `rd` lies in 0..31, `mem_write` is False on loads and True on stores, and
    `interrupt` is True if and only if `trap_cause` (`mcause` Bit 31 = 1) came from an
    asynchronous interrupt rather than a synchronous exception.
    """

    pc: int
    insn: int
    next_pc: int
    rd: int = 0
    rd_val: int = 0
    mem_addr: int | None = None
    mem_val: int | None = None
    mem_write: bool = False
    trap_cause: int | None = None
    interrupt: bool = False

Because each normal retirement writes at most one general-purpose register and at most one memory address while traps write none, those 10 fields capture every directly observable register, PC, memory, and trap transition of a single step. Trace FieldsPopulated On Normal RetirementPopulated On Trap / InterruptVerification Purpose

Two invariants close the verification loop opened in Section 1 (St+1=step(St)):

  1. Precise Exception Atomicity: Any step that traps leaves architectural registers, mac_acc, memory contents, and minstret untouched. Because Oracle.step() defers register writeback, PC updates, and minstret increments behind ExecOutcome and validates alignment, CSR permissions, and bus bounds before mutating memory, CSRs, or mac_acc, any step returning a non-None trap_cause enforces regst+1=regst, mac_acct+1=mac_acct, memt+1=memt, and minstrett+1=minstrett.
  2. O(1) Inductive Lockstep Sufficiency: Comparing the 10-field StepTrace receipt on every step verifies full register, pc, memory, and trap lockstep in constant work per step. Aside from deterministic per-step counter ticks (mcycle, mtime, and non-suppressed minstret), every non-trapping instruction mutates pc, at most one architectural register rd, at most one w∈{1,2,4}-byte memory or peripheral slice, and at most one CSR (mstatus on mret or the Zicsr target) or mac_acc register (including mac.clr x0, x1, x2, which updates mac_acc while discarding rd into x0). Starting hardware and oracle from identical reset state S0hardware=S0oracle under identical external peripheral inputs, step-by-step comparison of StepTrace therefore verifies pc, all 32 general-purpose registers, every memory write, and every trap transition in O(1) comparisons per step. In a conforming implementation, deterministic transition rules keep unlogged internal CSR, peripheral, and mac_acc state synchronized across steps; any hardware divergence in those internal registers surfaces in StepTrace as soon as a subsequent trap, mret, interrupt, non-x0 readback (csrrw, csrrs, csrrc, csrrwi, csrrsi, csrrci, lb, lbu, lh, lhu, lw, mac.get), or non-x0 mac writeback depends on it.
